CHARADES.
My first I hope you are, My second I see you are, My whole I know you are. Wei-roma:
My first is darkness, My second is a proposition, My third is a plant growing in bogs, Whole is the name of a bird. Nightingale.
My first is what all do after sleeating, my second is a plot of ground, my whole is•a`town in York- shire. Wakefield.
A very useful oren, Of the human trame ; Whichever way you read it, You'll find it is the same. Eye.
t.',Ty first gave us early support, My next is a virtuous lass : To the fields if at eve you resort, My whole you will probably pass. lir ilk-maid.
It seems to be in nature's plan The first should covt3r every man ; Last is a common stone Found everywhere, and whole is one On making money so intent He'd first my last to make a cent. Skin-flint.
You struggle up the mountain—hard work to reach
me; You fancy you are paid, so far around you see. But what a funny thing your eyes, perhaps, may meet ! A little boy has got me, and is playing in the street. Top.

No book without my first is made, However small or large; A boat my next which swiftly sails, And outstrips many a barge. My whole is used to cut my first, However thick it may be, A very useful thing am I, As quickly you will see. Paper-Cutter.

In winter's time my first is seen, When the weather is very Cold And is formed into my second By children young and old, And if my whole you wish to find, My first and second must be combined ; And then by looking you will see, A winter favourite in me.
,9now-bull.

A messenger, my whole who carries grief and joy. My whole is second, too; but not a frolicsome boy. Of stone or wood my first; and yet it spans th 4 globe, With messages untold, for palace and abode. Pose-nn.

A printer's term you'll find my first; Of mixed up things it is the worst. Second a fellow of low degree; Or, on mischief bent, a child may be. My whole, a thing of novel make— By Indians used on stream or lake. Pirogue.

div.head: GAMES.
div.p: GAMES.

THE readiest and most easily organised methods of amusing a mixed company arc "round games." The first point in starting round games is to choose a good leader. THE Comical. Cnonus.—Each member of the -party to sing one verse of any song, the rest of the party to follow with a chorus previously agreed upon. This may go round any numbeebf times, forfeits being paid by all who fail to sing. THE " MEDLEY."—One of the players is selected to tell a story. Each listener has to choose a "trade." When the story-teller requires a noun to be filled in he nods to the player addressed, who must supply an article out of his stock-in- trade. Forfeits may be demanded in this game. " MAGIC MCSIC."—One of the company leaves the room, and during his absence some article is hidden. On his return to search for it, a player at the piano commences a kind of musical com- mentary on his proceedings, growing louder as he approaches the hidden object, and fainter, as he recedes from it, the music thus guiding the searcher. " Hox COCELEA."—This is a variation of Blind Man's Buff. One of the players blindfolded kneels with his face hidden on a lady's lap, or the seat of a chair, and holds his open hands behind his back. The company then advance one by one, and each gives a slap on the extended palms; and the Blind Man is required to say whose was the hand that struck the blow. If he guesses right he is released, glid the striker takes his. place. Hum' nix RING. —A good large curtain ring, though not so large that it cannot be readily gidden in the hand, is procured. Through this ii threaded a piece of string five or six yards in length, the ends being joined so as to form an endless band. The company sit or stand in a circle, the cord passing through their closed hands. SANTA CLAUS;
A STORY OF Two CHRISTMAS EVES.
y CHARLES WINTHROP GRAHAM. -7:- CHAPTER L

The eve of Christmas in a busy street in-a large town, where you please. Snow falling heavily, the flakes like white-winged birds crossing and re. crossing each other at perplexing angles, and dart- ing hither and thither as if swayed by all kinds of strange impulses, and then vanishing voiceless into the tempest. The squat ugliness of the buildings huddled together in the bye streets is outlined in a a soft whiteness ; gaunt chimnies are crowned with fantastic minarets; dingy statutes are turned pie- bald by white patches on a black ground. Up and down the street, and round the corners, and in all the nooks and crevices hidden away in the dark streets where the closed warehouses cluster, careers the fierce wind—a very Bismarck of a wind, harsh, cruel, aggressive—searching out all unprotected places, and sending the drifted snow with an angry swirl in the places of foot passengers. "Seems to me people doesn't want no papers, nor nothing, now its Christmas 'eept turkeys and things ; and a pore lad might as well starve as try to get a honest livin', a selling evenin' papers." Thus in a hoarse voice, soliloquised a queer little figure, squatted with its knees up to its ch n, in a little alcove in one of the great public buildings of the town where we find ourselves. The wind whistled shrilly by, but with all its perseverance seldom found its way into this snug resting-place, and the snow only came in now and then with a vicious puff, that made the little object nestled up in the corner, shake the powdered particles from its face and head, impatiently and with a movement not unlike that of some animal. Leaning against the wall was a little crutch ; and beside the crutch was a bundle of evening papers. The owner of this property had screwed himself into so small a space, that almost all that could be seen beneath a hat of fearful and wonderful shape, was a broad, white face, which even a hasty glance showed, was of such complete and gratuitous ugliness, that one's first impulse on looking at it, was to shudder. A wide mouth with strong, capable teeth ; a low forehead, with knots of stubbly hair hanging over it in a straggling fringe; a nose, broken-bridged, probably with grief at the contemplation of its com- panion features; and—the most beautiful eyes that ever 100-ked out of an ugly head; tender, melting, fierce, appealing, as you watched them for a moment. "Ten o'clock ; and I've sold twelve, all this blessed night. And the people is all agoing 'ome with their baskets, and their Illustrated Newses and won't so much as look at the evenin's. And the snow's so thick on the ground that it soaks through my old boots like—like—anything. And the wind it's blowin' a good 'un. And the old man's await- ing at 'ome for me to take the money for his rum, afore he goes to bed. And I ain't got it. Ugh; there'll be merry Christians waitin for me, any how. 'Well, here goes, for another start." With a shiver, and a grunt, and many wonder- ful contortions, the strange figure rolled from its resting place, and alighted in the slush of the road- way. Then you could see that the hitleousness of of the face was more than equalled by the deformity of the body. The queer little object had no neck ; its chin pressed tightly on the collar-bone ; it had a hump on its back; and its two diminutive legs, though evidently strong, were warped and twisted. , The object walked with a side-long movement; and when using the crutch made prodigious speed. Its dress Was the va-Y acme a " looped and win- dowed raggedness ; " and bits of string peeped out here and there, giving the impression that they acted as kind of linch-pin to the whole structure, which would incontinently fall to piecess, imme- diately the sustaining element was removed. The only other noticeable thing in the grotesque, bizarre figure, was that its arms were long and muscular; and its chest might have been modelled on that of a Hercules. The little legs and the crutch skurried down the street at a tangent ; and the harsh, strident voice which their owner possessed, soon made itself heard and felt too, for its discordant notes pro- duced a sensation somewhat akin to that which one would feel when listening to a duet between a steam whistle and the hag-pipe. But it was a good serviceable voice ' • and when the dwarf darted under horses' heads, or penetrated into busses, or startled nervous ladies into a scream by popping up before them, apparently from a vampire trap let into the pavement, people bought from him, if not from curiosity, from pity. Therefore, it was not surprising that the crutch ere long felt that it had earned a little repose, and was soon clearing for itself a pathway in the snow, and going towards the recess where first we found it. " Peop'le allus buy off yer, if yer only holler loud enough, and stick to 'ern," meditated the Colonel (facetiously so called as a kind of graeefnl concession to the doctrine of contradictions, unconsciously laying down a commercial axiom which far greater people -than he, have followed with profit. "And now, afore I try to sell this last lot, suppose I has some supper. Taters is better'n pies, this weather; they're not so rich, but hotter. Lenone see,:,l can afford tuppence' so here goes. But 'ullo what's this?" He had reached his resting place, and there,, curled up, and fast asleep, he found a girl The Colonel's first feeling wasmne of indignation ; his next of curiosity. The girl, whoeyer she was, was sleeping the sleep of utter weariness. The Colonel saw at a glance, by standing on tiptoe that she was poorly clad; that her toes peeped bluely, through her old boots; that her thin dress and dilapidated shawl were pinned and " drawn together" aria patched, and darned. He saw too that her face was pretty, but white, and still; that her hair was fair,. and smoothly braided beneath an old bonnet which: might have been made for her grandmother. The, Colonel saw too, that she had in her hand a packet of what looked like lace, and that besides her lay some few coppers which had apparently slipped out of her pocket. He craned himself forward, as far as he could on his crutch, and stared with all his eyes at the sleeping girl. She coughed and , moaned in her sleep. "They most allus has coughs," murmured the Colonel philosphically. He still gazed with a puzzled air on the still white face;. and then I regret to say he deftly took the little parcel from. between her fingers, and gathering up the coppers lying on the floor slipped gently away chuckling with a chuckle that sounded like a Wagnerian symphony; and slapping his thigh apparently in an ecstacy of enjoyment. Ten minutes afterwards the sleeping occupant of the recess awoke, with a start, and after a struggle to realise where she was, felt for her parcel and her money, and missing both, began to cry. Then she thought she heard a hoarse, smothered laugh close to her, and became very frightened. Between = her sobs she had time to think that she had bettem get away from this place where invisible spirits laughed ghostly laughs, and made little girls afraid. , So she put one leg towards the ground, warily, bri' drew it back suddenly, as she saw a little, hideous,. humped-back man close to her, laughing in that diabolic manner which she had usually associated with expectant demons, " hanging7around", fur human souls. Then she saw the demon put his arms akimbo, s,nd assuming a severely judieial position say inn. , fearsome voice. "Look here, you. S'pose been a pleeceman, and seen you asleeping out. No means o' livelihood ; a 'bitual criminal, so to speak, what dyer s'pose I'd done? Why I'd took yer to . chokey ; that what I'd pone." The Colonel paused, as he saw that the chihr had covered up her face -with her hands, and was sobbing birterly. But altho' his eye-- seemed to soften in colour, and some few tender lines about , his mouth became more emphasised, he delivered himself of another Wagnerian chuckle, and con- tinued "I s'pose now,- it isn't likely you could ha' , been robbed, eh? nothing vallyable aboith yer t I No gold watch chains, net dimon rings, Dar parcels of lace, nor bank notes, nor copper, eh?' And, of course, yer can't be hungry, eh?' The girl, perhaps detecting some stOtle undo, tone in the hoarse voice, perhaps promlted by that wonderful divination whiCh teaches the poor to know their friends, looked up, and smiled a rain- bow smile, through her tears. 'I know I ougfitn't. to sleep here, but I was so tired. And (archly) you aren't a policeman I know; birt, (auspiciously) yi:?:r.,i've stolen my things. Tell me (naively) lerh nave ehae you ou The made no reply, but, edged slowly ur and quickly climbing up, disposed his tocruttebeh,eancerhis papers in the corner, and sitting besides the child, with his' elbows on his knees, and his ragged hat poked almost into her face, said with a deprecatory cough "I'm not going to criminate myself, as they says in the pleece courts, but s'pose you was to go to sleep for five minutes, and when you woke, you was to find yer parcel in yer hand, and yer money in yer pocket, what should ycr say?" "Why," said the child, smiling, "As it is Christmas, I should think Santa Claus had done

" Ah," pondered the Colonel, "some one y'know, likely ; that's been good to you. It's a queer name anyhow; sort o' furrin' sound about it. But if yer know him, it must be—it must be—all right I s'pose, eh ?" A pause, and then suddenly, "Well, here y'are ; put 'eni in yer pocket again. And now are yer hungry? I've noticed," said the Colonel medita- tively, and with the air of a commercial traveller pushing his wares, "I've noticed that at Christmas time people goes most on geese, and turkeys, and, taters. I aint got no geese, nor yit turkeys. But I've some tats. Twopennoth ; here they are, and, salt, here it is." He emptied his pockets hastily, and saying he would be back soon, left the child rigid with amazement, as the little crutch scattered the snow right and left on its way down the street.

CHAPTER 11. "I'll ask her who that Santa Claus is when I go' back," said the Colonel. " 'Pears to me she was chaffing. / never heard of him. Wonder where she lives ; and wonder would she let me walk home with her? Seems to white' like, and thin to a been long at that lace game. And a bad cough she has; but they most alias has coughs. Bad game that—lace. Papers is better ; so's needles and tape; so's anythink a'most. Lemme see, I've got three shillin's, and a dozen more to sell yet. I think I'll try the 'Crown.' There's pretty sure to he summun tight there, as 'll buy 'em up ; 'specially bein' Christmas Eve." He hoisted himself up the steps leading to the "Crown "—an hotel much affected by the gilded youth of the city; and made his way to the bar, where a number of that peculiar fungus growth of our civilization the bar exquisite, were exercising their vapid arts on a young lady of opulent charm;, possessing a face like a red potato—minus tit potato's genial expression. "What, ho I Colonel; my Apollo, my Goliah of Gath, my pocket Hercules what brings you out this Christmas Eve?" bawled out a jovial old gentleman with a red face, sitting in a corner, and puffing away at a long pipe, as if he wanted to blow his whole soul out at the bowl. "I want to sell these few, sir, afore I goes home." "So you shall, Colonel ; here's a shilling, and go straight home • and don't get winking at any of the girls you sly dog." The little crutch stumped blithely away after a carrulsive tug at a patch of rugged hair peeping from under the old hat, apparently for the express purpose of being pulled. Breathless, and with the intricate string and button arrangement of his alothing wofully disarranged, the Colonel returned to the place where he had left his companion. She was conaplacently finishing the last potato; and when he came up she put her hand in his as con- fidingly as if she had known him for a dozen years, and jumped down from the recess. The Colonel, in describing the scene in after times, was wont to enlarge upon his sensations when first he felt that little hand in his. "You're going home now, aint you," said the Colonel. "I'll walk with you some of the way; and we can look at the shops." "Yes," said the child readily, as she wrapped the shawl, a world too large, around her. "We an see the nice things Santa Claus will buy to for the children." "I say," said the Colonel, stopping abruptly in the roadway, "who is Santa Claus? 'Pears to me, he's a mighty curus sort o' cove. Have you known him long." "Why," said the child, in wonderment; "don't you know about him?' "No," said the Colonel, rather nettled; "how should I ?" " Well," said the child gravely, "he's a little man; a sort of fairy—a good one--who puts nice things in children's stockings on Christmas Eve. Some say he conies down the chimney, and some in at the window; but all I knows is, he does conic; and I always hang my stocking up on the window Ledge. But he hasn't been for a long time now; never since mother was ill, and we were poor." "Is he littler than me ; and is he—ugly,"queried the Colonel. "He's very little, I think, and he isn't at all pretty ; and he has a long white beard." wonder now," said the Colonel, meditatively stroking his chin, "if they all has beards ?" and then irrelevantly, "I say, what's your name ?" "Alice," said the child. "Alive," echoed the Colonel; "IV& a sweet name; / like it; and I shall often think of it, Alice." "Do if you like to," said the child. It was near midnight now, and they had: reached the nairow street in a distant quarter of the town, where the child lived. The snow had ceased fall- ing, and the moon was lighting up the shabby out- lines of the houses with an altogether unmerited glory, touching too the two lonely figures with an infinite compassion. "I live here," abruptly said the child, an they stopped at the entrance to a narrow court. "'Have you far to go ?" "Oh, no; close to," replied the ColOnell, with ready untruthfulness. After a pause, as if with a sudden inspirszlim, and laughing a trifle wildly, he said, "Look here, about this Santa Claus. I think you and me, oars have a little game. S'pose you says to your mother when you goes in, Mother,' says you, kind o care- less like, I wonder if Santa Claus 'll come. M- night t' 'No,' says she, 'course not.' P'raps,' says you, accidental like, if I hang my stockin' up, and leave the winder open, he -may coma" • Rubbish,' says she. But you hangs it up, all the same„ and—and—then, well, it'll be all right thus, won't it—eh ?" "Bat I'm sure he won't come." "Look here," resumed the Colonel sententionelaja. "You say this Santy Claus is a little man. What comes in at the winder. And he's ugly. pi'sapa he,s lame too. Yer can't tell. 'T any rate Its. ugly. Well, if he was round in this street, and yen: hang anst yer stockin' on the winder ledge, and kave, the winder open, he gets natural like on that avali,, he step on that bottom shutter, he pulls hisself up. by his hands, and he finds the stoelsiss', and hsi.pptis. in may be, a necklace. And there y'zire." "Oh, no no he won't," replied tha girl shiseririgs in. the cold, and tucking up her bt shawl under her arm pits, "I never expect himsnow ; ,Isdoulta think Ise comes to poor people like 113." "Well, I clunno," said the Coloael in a tene. &- reflection; "1 any rate, lets hope: he will." He took her hand in both his, and steasdied himself on,. his crutch whilst he stroked it softly; and thenthe silence was broken by something, very like,a sob, and when the moon next threw a silver pencil oE.. light under the slouching brim of the Coloael's hair it found in his eyes, oddly enougi,—tears, . "1 must go now," said the child, gentlrytakimg her hand away, "Good merry Christnia& to yon." She turned away, walked slowly for a Lmw yarflia, as if moved by a sudden impuls-seamequ'ekly back and kissed him on the cheek and brow; befmm he had raised his head she was gone. Half an hour later the Col mei stumped intaaa shop which had a gorgeous disiplay of Birmingham ware in the window, climbed deliberately on to a high stool, placed four shillinT on the counter ao€l said in, a voice which made tie shopman starkaas if he had been detected in roblisag the till, "The necklace in the window; the Mass- and. -gold; one; its four shilling; there's the money," It was but a paltry( to at best a tawdry and brassy and worthless; buts the Colonel handled it tenderly as if it were a revelation of rare beauty, anillaviug had it put,lntoaa little bax, hid it away in. some inner pocket. . -a 5 • 5. The wall was hard to olimb, anti the long arms were bruised, and the, hands scratched as the Colonel, with a face white with esseitement dropped to the ground, and Tess-reed his crutch, j&ast as the stoke of midnight pealed forth on, the still air. But the little box was lying snugly in the worn stock- ag ; and Alice slept on, all unaonscioua,that Santa mama, weary and worn, but with a wild thrill at his heart, and a tender light its his epee lay awake,, and lemming day dreams in his squalid bed until the grey dawn of Christmas morning crept shads bring across the sky.
CHAPTEU

Christmas p d,;ithils ever shifting kaleido- scope of joys and sorrows.; of present griefs, and even sadder remembrances ; of wretchedness made leas wretched,, and prosperity more prosperous by the hallowing, influence of that happy time. And then, when the new year had passed people gradu- ally sank ba.k into their old groove of occupation; and anothex year's struggling for many weary of the battle,, had commenced, The Colonel had gradually despite many rebuffs (for the bed-ridden mother of Alice was one of those peevish, inconse- quent women who could bear prosperity with a sweet gentleness, but whom poverty made unjust and exacting and occasionally cruel) had established himself almost as an ex officio member of the small household, He was a hewer of wood, and a drawer a water, and carrier of messages ; and every moment of his day, before he commenced his even- h scant seated on a stool at the &re-

sicie—wnen ine-fis"was-a-rife, wincn vtas not always —carving quaint monstrosities out of wood with a jack-knife, and some how always finding a sale for the articles ehen they were finished. He listened patiently and gave the sympathy of his eyes and his silence to the sick woman's stories of her rich surroundings in days gone by. He did not pry into the history of the skeleton which occupied the cupboard, even of this poor family; but gradually got to believe that the father was expiating some bye-gone folly—it never reached to crime—abroad; and that it was within the bounds of possibility he might return at any time, and restore his wife and family to their old position. The Colonel amongst his other qualities possessed those of patience, of perseverance and of method. He incessantly haunted all the small ware shops in the city until he found an established sale for all the lace the bed- ridden woman could make. After a hard battle he set up Alice as a sales-woman of evening papers to regular customers at the expense of many a fight d out rance with the rather turbulent constituency with whom she had to compete. Every night he called for her; robed her carefully in her tattered shawl, and went out with her "to business," re- turning with her, late or early as business had prospered, or otherwise. And the child accepted the companionship with a quiet gravity and trust- fulness which sat oddly and yet appropriately upon her. So the months sped on; and despite their poverty this trinity of outcasts were not unhappy, and if the Colonel had of late taken to long fits of abstrac- tion, and the light in the dreamy eyes had softened and grown tender, it was not because he was un- happy; and the timid embarrassed, almost womanly manner which had grown upon him and not suit him ill. "Alice "he said, one night, as they stood hand in hand, on the threshold of her mother's door, " summun told me once that people all 'ad a good angel, as followed 'em about, and kept it's eye on 'em like; 'an was allus with 'em when they was happy and when they wasn't. Sort o' Santa Claus like t only allus look in' in at the winder. I wonder whDis yours; I know who's mine." "I should think," said the girl softly, and with her eyes on the ground " that you were mine. You are so good, and kind, and—and—l always think of you. Dolyou think if I wanted you to, very, very, much, you could always think of me on Christmas Eve, when Santa Claus comes—and when—when—l first met you. Could you, even if I were away from you--or—or dead." He drew her gently to him, and pressing her head down on his misshapen shoulder, whispered " Allus, allus, I can never forget you, even for a day." Then he kissed her gently, almost reverently, and Moved quickly away. The next day he went at nightfall to the house and found it closed. Bewildered, he peeped in at the window, and rattled the latch. No answer. A sudden chill came over him, and he was standing gazing vacantly at the darkened windows, when he hearda woman saying to him, "Here young 'un ; a note for you." The Colonel had never received a note before, and he could not read;. but he looked at the mysterious looking document in all lights and in all angles. Then he hurried off down the street till he meet a policeman. "See yer. Read me this will yer. no scholard.' There were only a few lines irethe crumpled note; hut it told "in characters uncouth, and spelt amiss," that "Pa has been and took us away in a carriage, and were going to be rich, now." And they told "him not to forget his promise; and sent him much love, and concluded " your lbving Alice." "There, will that do for yore,"said the pol:ee- man, handing him back the erumpled piece: of paper. "Yes" he said wearily, and as- if scarcely cetts scious of what he was saying. "-I s'pose I'd better go now, there's nothing to keep me here. And it seems getting dark and cold. And my head ia swimmirg round like." He moved away and that street knew him no more. Months passed and winter drew' near; In the -duff November days the winds seemed to have in them, a mournful note, as if sighing a requiem over they dying year, and all nature seemed hushed au& I dead. "An' yen saw 'er with yer over eyes," said thw Colonel to•a rough fellow standing besides him,. " Didn't 1 just," replied the person addressed.. "When yea arst me, after you ad found out thes place to look out for 'er if I was in that' neighbour-- hood, of oceerse I did, Feu bein' Colonel, a good sort, let alime a cripple. They lives in a big; 'ouse I can tell yer. Gardens in front, an' trees, an' lawns, and roses, and honeysuckle trailin' all up the front:of the 'ouse. Well, as .Lwas a-lookin" at it all, who should drive up ire a little pony' carriage, bet. 'er. She was leanin'Thack, weary- like, and were wrapped up in furs an' things, and was a coughia? as if it would tear her 'to pieces." " Ah," said, the Colonel, " they- most allus has. coughs. Sheallus had. Go on." " Well st,a, wer' lifted out ancl; carried up to. the house ; and look here Colonel, strike me if ever I saw a girl 4S- looked like dyin', skit did. Why Colonel, wot ethe matter. The GOlOll4 had staggered bacl4.lais hand on. his forehead, hie face deadly white, his eyes wild and staring. "'What d'yerenean," he shoutede. "You're a. liar, you've been put on to tell me- this by her father as won tact me see 'er, or -.wile to 'Cr, or' remember 'er lie can help it. D him." He paused suddenly and then burst ir.iSa tearing sobs. that shook him .11.ead to foot. Christmas lire again. A little eil?age nestling under the calso, shadow of the meuntains of the Peak. Mountain and meadow, woodland and moorland, cottage and mansion, clothed in a mantle of deal, unvarying white. The moon clearing a silvery pathwap through the snow flakes, and a solemn stillness over all, wive where the night breeze bore in graduated maody to the ear' the strains of Christmas carols, sung at far oir farm houses. "I'm very tired, and somehow- the old crutch, seems to drag heavy to-night. Just when it-, shouldn't. An' it's a long, long„way from there- station. But never mind, it's gettin' on for 12' o'clock, and lesi here now. Whene was I this time • last year; where was she ; where shall we both ba. next year? It does seem so long since, 'an som'ow - I wish it all 'ah to come over again. Don't forget.. yer promise- she said. I aint forgot it. And then she said, 'I think you're my good, angel.' I wish I was, but 'er father won't let me.. He can't keep Santa Clans out, tholigh, on Christmas. Eve, can be ? ' He had reached the entrance, gate to the hums standing back from the road, and the dim outlive) of which could be seen in the- shadow. The trim flower bed* the smooth lawn,. the dark box edging were all covered with snow,. and the evergreens threw long black patches, on ,the clear whiteness of the ground. He crept stealthily along through the little avenue of trees which veiled the approach, to the house. The blinds were, down, and aTh the windows facing to the lawn, were dark save•one. He did not notice this, or in fact any other of his surroundings, but kept his face towards the.dight, ' with a pitiable eagerness whieh expressed ithseff in law gasps. "That's her window' Iknow," he said, "and all seems cptiet and still. Wonder if the little stock. ing'tethere, like it watilast y,ear Wonderif she's thinking of me? I think, if I was her, I cot:ldlest!! somehow, Santa Clautewas near. Here,* taking ee little packet from his pocket, is what I've brought. her.. 'Tisn't much, and. pampa she donit care.for,- suds things now—as she used to, but shew 'en• I don't forgit her. Am? the little Chrismas card L get too. That's pretty 'tanyrate ; an' has angels,— angels with fair hair and beautiful faaes,.like *ere,, bless 'er." He stopped and' kissed the little packet, andthem moved rapidly ontowards the house. The f rent el the building was cay.ered with brattice-work, up which boneysuelcle and roses,. climbed and blossomed ia the glad summer time. He crept up it with, ease, and clinging to the, window sill, and holding en. with his feet to the, brattiee-work, looked intAhe room. He saw two, figures; one a woman,, sobbing round the neck of a mane whose 'lair was grey and whose face was seamed with cruel lines cut by the, chisel of time, and, leng•suffering and repentance.. The light burned low, and had a great blue ring round it; and the iceman's ache sounded with awful distinctness. Then the man's voice, low and trembling, and sounding to the listening ears at the window, a long way elf, murmured something about "our poor dead darling," and ended in a groan; and both of them, bending down kissed something reverently, as it lay upon the bed, and slowly left the room. The clinging figure outside, in a strange, dazed way, brushed its hair from its face; and then peered with all its eyes through the crevices of the blind. She was lying, with a smile on her face and her little thin hands crossed on the white eoverlid before her, with her fair hair brushed smoothly off her fair brow, like it was when he had. first seen her ; and in her cheek there was the same dimple that was always there. But there was no hacking cough now ; no groaning in this last soft sleep. The face. with the uncertain shadows thrown lot
r,

trie ni'cr.ering lignt playing upon it, secineu now laughing, now thoughtful, but always beautiful; and if it be true, as some say, that the face of the dead always assumes the expression of its happier and younger days, then the end of this frail flower indeed was peace. It might have been a minute, or an hour, that the figure watched, with white face and straining eyes, at the window; but at last the darkness of the night was stabbed by a wild unearthly cry of agony and grief; and the object clinging to the wall threw its arms wildly round, fell backwards, turned over once, twice, thrice, and struck with a sickening thud on the sharp peaks of an ornamental rocket' below. The cry was heard; and the Colonel was carried, bleeding and insensible, into the house. The verdict of the doctor when he came was brief and stern: there would be a brief period of conscious- ness andlthen the end. The period of unconscious- ness might be long or short, but it could only have one termination..

In the middle of the night, when the watchers were pale and weary with their vigil, the Colonel opened his eyes, and said calmly, and with no trace of pain,. "Will ye,r it me see—her. Once; only ones." They took him into the little room, and propped him up in a chair close to the bed, with the bereaved father and mother beside him.

" I don't want," he said, weakly, and taking her mother's hand, in his, "-to say much about—her--- now. She's in Heaven; lookin' down on us, likely nuff. But I'd like to say as. 8114 wanted me to come here this Christmas Eve;. and so, you see, o' course', I come. What could I do, different? She said I was 'Cr good angel—and—and she kissed me. An' some'ow it didn't seem so cold,. an' lonely, an' ard then. An' when she went,away I allus seemed to see her afore me saying, 'Santa Claus. A little man. Ugly; p'raps lame: Comes in at the winder.' Santa Claus came to her once;. she knew who 'twas then. An' now, now she's, with the angels, he's come agin, not knowin' as she'd gone. An' I think he's anus goin' to stop with 'Cr mow. P'raps say a word for the poor,.little,,ugly lad wot loved her so dear; and there may be room up there, even for 'ins. That's all PVe.got,to say. Lift me up, and let me kiss her just once, and then say those words she used to say. 'bout. 'suffer little chil- dren to come unto inc.'" They raised him up, andle softlykissecl the white brow, and then with a long, happy sigh, fell back into their arms—dead. "Truly," said the grey-haired man, standing hand-in-hand with his wife, and looking on the two dead faces, "of such is the kingdorroof Heaven."

PRIDE OF "'Er H E MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAVRA JEAN LIBBEI.
CHAPTER XL.

THOSE WO HAVE WORKED FOR BREAD REJOICE IN A WORKING GIRL'S TRIUMPH. As Arthur had said, the' physicians could not find It in their hearts to refuee his request, and they were ushered straightway into lonie's presence. The doctor's wife had arrayed her with great care for their coming. She had dressed her in a dress of soft pink mull, with, soft, white lace a the neck and throat, garnishing the simple but strik- ingly becoming costume with a cluster of pale pink blossoms at the belt, and twined among the nut- brown curls.

Arthur would have entered alone, but his com- panions thought it would be best not to allow him to do so, and accompanied him, For one instant Arthur stood on the threshold, bewildered by the vision of girlish beauty in the great willow rocker at the window, which met his gaze. "lonie I my darling!" he cried; and with one bound he was by her side. But, ah, Heaven, the pity of 2W The pity of it There was no look of recognition in the lovely dark eyes that met his own for a moment, and wandered past him. "Oh, my God,. Tonics, don't you know me?" he cried, in such agony that the strong men who accompanied him tamed away with tears standing in their eyes, "Oh, this is toes horrible—tee horrible?" he groaned. "Have I lost you only to find you like this? Death could not have been much worse. Look at me, darling! Hear me speak! Try to recognise me." But he might as well have talked to the waving trees outside. Some one touched bins on the shoulder. It was one of the physicians. "Let me persuade you to come away, Mr. Rochester,Thile we make our examination to see if the young lady's case is inded hopeless," he said. "your grief can avail her nothing—our assistance might; I cannot tell." With his eyes blinded tears, Arthur followed the doctor's wife into an adjoining parlour, and she then excused' herself to return to lonie's side. If seemed to Arthur that 'he paced the confines of that narrow little room long hours. And yet the examination was not over; they had not come to tell him the result. He could not endure the suspense one moment longer; crossing the hall, hte tapped nervously yet softly upon the door. Dr. Wright opened it, and if Arthur had not been so agitated he would have noticed at once that the doctor's face looked unusually grave. "How does the case stand?" asked Arthur, eagerly. "You can effect a cure, can you not 2" "Let us come out under the trees, and we will talk the matter over/' replied the doctor, evasively. Together they • walked Mr' down through the fragrant, old-fashioned garden, rich with a wilder- ness of flowers, and odorous 'with the honey of the bee-hives. "You brought me out hereto speak," said Arthur, impatiently, "but you do nolaseem in any hurry to! begin." "I am trying to find word§ to begin that which I have to say," said the doctors. who was always so plentiful with his ideas. With these words _hue left Arthur, The moments that passed Arthurßochesterdneaer forgot while- his life lasted. The agony of sanrest was. on him, He paced the path from- the lilac bush down to wirsere the roses grew at thedorther end, of( the- garden, with quick, impatient- strides. She was a great lady; but, ahl she would always be the friend of the poor working- girls; and as she stepped into her carriage, and took her seat beside her proud and happy husband, a mighty cheer rose up, as with one accord, from the groups at the doors and windows of the Nottingham Mills, and they cried from the depths of their hearts:

div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Lady Egerton of Tatton's death will be much re- gretted in Cheshire, where she lived. There was not a kinder hostess or more public-spirited woman in the county. Benevolent social schemes seldom appealed to her in vain. Among other things she took a keen interest in the Girl' Friendly Society, of which she was president. Lady Egerton's use- ful life had extended to fifty-six years, thirty-five of which had been years of happy union with her husband. Lady Egerton's only child is the wife of Viscount Bury.

The circumstances that induced Captain Arm- strong, alias "Kangaroo Charley," to withdraw the proceedings for divorce that he initiated against his wife (Madame Melba) and the Duke of Orleans (co-respondent) have not been allowed to tianspire. A Sydney contemporary, to hand by Tuesday's Asstralian mail, says :—" There are various wild rumours about as to the terms upon which ' Char- ley' Armstrong has withdrawn his petition for divorce against Madame Melba, but no one who knows the • Kangaroo' would suppose for a moment that he would make a commercial speculation of such a thing."

On Sunday night there died the oldest solicitor en the rolls. He was ninety years of age, and if it be true that " lawyers take one step towards Heaven in seven years," Mr. George Harvey Mirfin was able to go further in that direction than most men of his profession. His was an eventful as well as a prolonged existence, and long ago he was not only a prosperous practitioner, but also a popular M.P.H., a combination of affairs which is seldom found in these driving days. He made his name in the West of England, and was little known in Lon- don, where he ended his days,in small and secluded chambers in Staple-inn.

An enterprising agent has prepared for the use af theatrical managers printed list of the names of the dramatic critics and the newspapers to which they are accredited. It need hardly be said that this is done without authority, and that the list is by no means free from mistakes. It is surprising to find that there are more than two hundred the- atrical critics in London, and the number does not include the ladies who " do " the dresses, or the host of London correspondents who follow the drama in the interests of theprovincial and colon- ial and even the suburban press.

A man of any public spirit would hardly choose the present time to drive the sheep from agreat ex- panse of Scottish pasture and turn it into a deer forest. The injury done to the Highlanders by these clearances and enclosures was never more generally admitted than it is just now, and only on Saturday the duties of the new Commission on Deer Forests were officially explained. Yet on the eve of this announcement we learn that Lord Abinger has bought twenty thousand acres of sheep pasture in Inverness-shire, and means to turn it into a deer forest. Lord Abinger will not gain much by thus launting his indifference to public opinion in the face of the country.

Mr. Fred Burbridge, who has just died at the age of sixty, was the wealthy member of a large City Arm of wholesale druggists, Burgoyne, Burbridge, and Cyriax, whose working partner, by the way, Mr. Julias Cyriax, well known in musical circles and an enthusiastic Wagnerite, died in Norway en his holiday only a! few weeks ago. Mr.'Fred Bur- bridge was better known in sporting than in City circles. He was fond of horses and an excellent judge of horseflesh. But his principal triumphs bad been won in the cricket field. Of about the middle height, and very strongly built, with a keen eye and capital wrist, Mr. Burbridge was a well- known member of the Surrey county team as long ago as 1854, when the Eleven was captained in many a victory by Mr. F. P. Miller. Mr. Burbridge who had been for some time in failing health, died at his charming country seat Micklefield, near Itickmansworth.

Lord Portarlington, who died on Saturday at his house at Bournemouth, at the age of sixty, was in early life an officer in the Guards, and saw service in the Crimean campaign. For nearly three-and- twenty years, as Mr. Lionel Dawson-Damer, he sat es M.P. for Portarlington in the Conservative inte- rest, and succeeded to the title comparatively lately. He was the representative of two ancient families the Damers, of Dorsetshire, and the Dawsons, of Queen's County, Ireland. He certainly did not in- herit his Conservative opinions from his ancestor, Joseph Darner, who took up his abode in Ireland on the restoratior of Charles 11., for that gentleman was a thick and thin ,supporter of Cromwell. The Dawson who married a Darner in the early part of last century, and thus secured for his deAcendants the succession to the Darner properties, was M.P. for Portal lington, and later for .Queen's Coup ty.

The Earl of Portarlingi on, who died at Bourne- mouth on Saturday, had been an invalid for many years. At one time there waa no maore popular man in London society. He was then 'known as " Hippy" Darner, and sat for the family borough of Portarlington during two Parliaments, to the ad- miring wonder of those who knew his political qualifications best. Of late he had lived mainly, out of London. He succeeded to the earldom three years ago on the death of his eccentric cousin, whose; executors were instructed with all his Tinge on his Angers. The Portarlington estates extend to twenty- oix thousand acres, chiefly in Tipperary, and are valuable as Irish properties go.

The sensation of the hour in Catholic circles is the wholly unexpected secession of the Rev. Dr.^William Sullivan, who, during the past four years has been one of the most popular preachers and one of the ablest controversialists in Catholic London. Ile has been somewhat silent for the past few months, but it was generally understood that he was about to be promoted to the charge of a parish, as he had got tired of professional work at the Diocesan Seminary in Haramersmith. That he had lost faith in the orthodaxy which he was wont to expound from almost every Catholic pulpit in London was a thought that never once occurred to his host of admirers. No London priest was SO well and 60 widely known, for his professional duties left him entirely free on Sundays, and he was thus enabled to deliver courses of sermons at various Catholic churches in succession. Sometimes he would address a-wealthy and fashionable congregation in the morning at the Pro-Cathedral, Kensington, and the evening of the same day would find him preach- ing on a different subject altogether to a gathering of workingmen and working-women at the East- end.

Dr. Sullivan's seccession is undoubtedly the severest blow that London Catholicism has received , since Cardinal Manning silenced Monsignor Capel. Like the latter, Dr. Sullivan was instrumental in securing converts by the score. Of Irish parentage he was gifted with many of the graces of Hibernian oratory. He was exceedingly fluent, had a singu- larly persuasive style, possessed a marvellous mem- ory that enabled him to clinch his argument with the right quotation at the right time without any reference to notes, and was endowed with an exceptionally musical and sympathetic voice. At Rome, where he studied for the priesthood and was ordained, be acquired large stores of erudition, and was well grounded in all the essentials of a great and ready Catholic controversialist. His doctor's degree was not the mere honorary university dis- tinction that it usually is in England ; he gained it in Rome by hard study and a brilliant public exhi- bition of his controversial talents.

Miss Lucy Booth, who is lying dangerously ill in tndia, is General Booth's youngest daughter. She is a tall, slight girl, with dark hair and eyes, and a very intellectual face. Miss Lucy Booth has not been very strong for a year or two—at least, she has not been robust. A short visit she paid to In- dia when her eldest sister was there did her much good. It was therefore thought that the Indian climate would suit her, and it is to be hoped that the expectation may yet prove well founded. Miss Booth is practically at the head of the Salvation Army in India, and she has taken a native name.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
SALTPORT.

Saltport is at present little Tmore than a name on the Ship Canal map, and it will says the " Manchester Guardian," probably be a few years before it secures any recognition from the general cartographer. The baptism of the port was quite a recant affair. It was, as a matter of fact, not till the month of July last that Saltport was called into a nominal existence, and so descriptively styled. On a day in that month the Chair- man of the Salt Union, a corporation which owns a great fleet of barges, sailed up the Mersey and entered the Canal at Eastham. He navigated the canal for a dis- tance of ten miles to the place marked on all Parliamen- tary plans of the waterway as" Point A," where for the present the completed works end ; and, throwing a long slender bottle of Hockheimer of rich colour against some stakes in the water, proclaimed the place to be Saitport. At the time of the christening ceremony there was little or nothing to mark out this spot from any other on the Canal. There was the broad line of water, within call of the Mersey, and all around, except for the wide and shallow pool into which the spent forces of the Weaver empty themselves, the green fields and wooded slopes of Cheshire. But to-day there is much more La stimulate the imagination. About a score of boats, from near 5,000 tons register down to craft of 700 tons, are discharging cargoes at Saltport during this present week. The Jan Melchers brings pitchpine and oak from Mobile; the Penwortham, an old Ribble boat, has a fine load of sugar, which will shortly find its way to Withy Grove ; there are consign- ments of varied stuffs from the Baltic regions, from the southern seas, and from our possessions in the far-off parts of the Western hemisphere. Moreover, the visitor who runs over to Saltport for a day—if he be so fortu- nate as to overcome the difficulties of the journey—will see the repeated opening of a swing bridge which marks a narrow channel in the Weaver Pool, and the passage into the canal of barges containing salt and chemicals and the purple ore which is used in the puddling of iron. One feature of ordinary life Saltport is strangely in need of. Not a single house or habitable place has yet been built. All who live in Saltport live in the ships which come there. The labouring population who attend to the steam cranes which unload theiships and the workers who perform various and miscellaneous duties have their homes at Runcorn, a couple of miles away. The railway train brings them to their work early in the morning, returns with them at noon for their meals, and when night falls again conveys them to their homes. Bat this state of things will soon be altered. Since the Latchford section of • the canal was finished there are wooden dwellings which are no longer tenanted, and these are to be planted on Saltport soil, so as to conduce to the economy of labour. When that change takes place the men will be unable to flock, as this week they do, to the little theatre at Runcorn, where the realism of a Ship Canal drama with strong situations is considerably aided by the flooding of the stage with real water. Saltport, as we have said, has no location on the maps of the world. This fact has lately led to the bewilder- ment of traders. Two months ago the steamship Helen lay at Pensacola, In the Mexican Gulf, loading a cargo of pitchpine timber. The captain telegraphed to his owners that the merchants—who had the option of ordering the vessel to any safe port in the .United Kingdom—destined him for Saltoort. In return the owners in Belfast found I it necessary to wire to Pensacola that they might be ',old where Saltport was. Mr. Marshall Stevens,the manager of the Ship Canal Company, is doing what he can rapidly to dissipate ignorance of this sort. Far and wide he is circulating a pretty little handbook, prepared in a dis- tinctly American style,which should convince all traders and honest mariners that Saltport has a satisfactory existence. From this book it may be seen at a glance what the ship dues are for a vessel with cargo from different parts of Great Britain, from the northern regions by the Cattegat and White Sea, or the southern lands below Cape Finisterre. It may be hoped that when , this knowledge has had time to grow from more to more the trade of Saltport will expand until there are not twenty ships merely in its broad inland waters, but a fleet with cargoes of choice goods from all parts of the world. It may reassureehippers who do not know the dimensions of the Canal and how capacious its accom- modation to learn that three Atlantic liters are to be berthed in it during the winter months. The Beaver line steamer Lake Ontario entered the Eastham locks yesterday. The gross register of this vessel i 54,502 tons, its length is 375 ft., its breadth 43ft., aud its depth 291 t. The Lake Nepigon should fellow to-day, and the Lake Superior, which has a length of 400 ft. and a gross regis- ter of 4,562 tons, will enter the Canal later on. These three boats, it may be mentioned, are resting because of bad trade and of the immigration restrictions which are being imposed by the United States. Ordinarily they would be berthed in a dock at Liverpool, but the Beaver Company find it to their advantage to make the change. It may be interesting to state, In this.connection, that during this present week of neap tides there is a greater depth of water in the Ship Canal at Saltport than there is in any dock in Liverpool. The ambition of the founders of Saltport has grown very considerably since last July. The original func- tion of the place was of quite a modest sort. It was one of the provisions of the -Ship Canal Act that the docks at Runcorn should not be interfered with nor certain other works commenced rbetween Runcorn and the Weaver Pool until the Canal between Eastham and the river Weaver had been completed and opened for Wee. The Canal Company were also bound by the provisions of the Act to supply themanufacturers of the town, after the closing of the docks, with their pottery materials and the other articles which came to them by way of the Mersey exactly as they had been in the habit of receiving them. The manufac- turers were, in short, properly guarded by Parliament from any inconvenience to their trade caused by the making Tof the Canal. Having finished and npened their ten miles of waterway, the Company closed the Runcorn docks last July, and in order to comply with their Act they leased the docks at Weston Point. Here they received the Mersey boats bound for Run- corn and sent on their cargoes in Urges. It was thought well to supplement this provision by estab- lishing a port on the Ship Canal itseelf, where the goods for Runcorn could be discharged and carried away in waggons to their destination. ,For this primary purpose was it that what is known on the Ordnance survey plans as "Lordships Marsh" was, turned into what is now a small centre of shipping.' The design of Mr. Stevens and his cdtleagues has grown on their hands. Saltport, it was quickly found, ,could not only serve Runcorn, but Manchester also, while at the same time its establishment might accustom vessels to the navigation of the Canal. If Messrs, Berisford find it cheaper and equally con- venient to get their sugar by way of Saltport rather than by Liverpool, there seems little reason why the example should not be followed by other traders. The conveniences for loading and unloading could not easily be improved upon. Within the fine width of the Canal runs a jetty some 700 feet long. There is room for the biggest ships in the world between the ' jetty and the Mersey bank of the Canal ; while a narrower way, N feet wide with a depth of 12 feet of water, runs between the jetty and the nearer shore. The narrow way is for the convenience of barges which use the small navigations inland. On the jetty are half-a-dozen steam cranes, by means of which unloading is accomplished with great despatch. As an instance of quick work it may be mentioned that between the morning of one day and the evening of the next 1,100 tons of farina were discharged from the steamship Berlin into flats. When it is further stated that Saltport has a vast storehcuse and that the Weaver Pool forms one of the finest timber ponds in the world, the possessions and conveniences of the place may be said to be fairly summed up. In the days to come Saltport may possibly become a com- petitor with Ellesmere Port and Runcorn. It has al- ready been explained that the latter town is for the time being placed under some inconvenience by the making of the Ship Canal. When, however, the Canal is made Runcorn will be so well equipped that it may confidently expect a large increase of trade. The Mersey did not serve its turn at all well. Once a boat was docked with its cargo, it was very uncertain when the tide would allow of its return. When the Ship Canal is open Runcorn may receive boats several times the size of any that it has known in the past, and tides will be no longer a matter of any moment to the owners.

The financial statement was submitted, the accept- ance of which appears in the Committee's report, given hereafter.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that it had always been an anxiety on the part of the committee of manage- ment to bring the total funds account np to £300,000, but they had never got quite up to that amount. He might explain that that was due in a great measure to the fact that people with £lOO or over that amount to invest, generally put it into Government securities, so that when they drew £lOO or more out of the bank, it made the amount standing there less. He moved that the statement of accounts prepared by the actuary, and examined by the auditor be approved, and copies there- of directed to be transmitted to the national debt com- missioners, and to the committee of inspection appointed I under 1891 Act, and that a duplicate statement be pub- licly affixed to the Savings Bank.—The Vice-Chairman seconded, and the motion was adopted. THE COMMITTEE'S REPORT.—THE UTILITY OF MANAGERS. _ _

The CHAIRMAN read the annual report of the Commit- tee of Management, which was as follows :—" The Com- mittee of Management in presenting the general state- ment of the bank for the year ending 20th November, 1892. have to report that—the total funds amount to £296,885 us. 4d., as under: With the National Debt Commissioners—on general account, £291,749 16s. lid.; on separate surplus fund account, carrying interest, £1,400; on separate surplus fund account, not carrying interest, £700; £293,849 16s. lid.; with Joseph Charl- ton Parr, Esquire, treasurer, £3,015 14s. 5d.; £298,865 11s. 4d.; the total amount due on 10,734 deposit account is £293,788 16s. Bd. ; leaving a surplus of £3,076 14s. Bd. The above plainly shows that the Government have in hand on account of this bank more than would pay the depositors the amount due to them, and that with the amount in the treasurer's hands, there is the large sur- plus of £3,076 14s. Bd., and there is the value of the bank premises. The Government also hold £11,645- 21 per cent, consolidated stock on account of depositors in this bank. New rules, prepared in conformity with the Acts of Parliament, have been issued to depositors on their attendance at the bank. Any depositor not having had a copy may have one on application. By the Savings Bank Act, 1891, depositors are now allowed to re-deposit any sum previously withdrawn in the same year, beyond the £3O deposit limit; and also are allowed to deposit in the whole up to £2OO instead of £l5O as heretofore. The Committee would point out to deposi- tors and to all provident people who have not hitherto used the bank, that although the security for the money lodged was beyond all doubt (the -Government always having to the credit of this bank more than would pay every depositor in full), the passing of the new Act even makes the position of the bank stronger than before, as a Government Inspection Committee is now appointed under which an Inspectoi• periodically inspects this and other Savings Banks, and sees that the requirements of the Acts of Parliament are properly carried out. The extracted list of depositors' balances certified by the auditor, is placed on the bank counter during the hours of business, and any depositor may personally satisfy himself that the same amount as is in' his pass book is certified to the Government as being to his credit. A copy of the Government certificate is printed with this report and the original may be seen at the bank by any depositor desiring to see it. The Committee are pleased to report that we have now over ten thousand deposi- tors and would impress upon them the desirability of continuing to increase their deposits and to promote amongst their friends the beneficial practice of saving and using this bank.—For the Committee of Manage.- ment, JOHN R. PICEMERE, Chairman; Was. LONG, Vice- Chairman. 6th December, 1892. The MATOR moved that the report of the Committee of Management be approved, and that the meeting acknowledge the valuable services, to the institution of the actuary, and the gentlemen acting on the committee during the past year, and tender them the best ;thanks of the meeting.—Mr. Roberts seconded. He said lie should like to ask a question, though he did so in all kindness, as to a matter on which he was in doubt. What use the managers of the institution, as managers, now were. He remarked that there were times when managers were required to give their attendance at the bank during the hours in which it was open, but, that n)w he did not know what their responsibilities and duties consisted of. He asked if they were there merely for purposes of ornamentation. Perhaps it was desirable to keep them even in that capacity, but the matter was open to doubt and consideration.—Mr. FLEMING said he had almost intended to ask the same question. In CORl- ing upstairs he spoke to Mr. Davies on the subject. The managers were only called there once a month, and he did not know whether that constituted being a manager. He had never seen a piece of paper or been asked to attend a meeting as to the bank's affairs during the year He thought a mere ornament was not a very useful thing. He supported the motion.—The CHAIRMAN said the very words Mr. Roberts and Mr. Fleming used justified the appointment of managers. All managers were entitled to attend any meeting of the bank, the annual meeting or the committee meetings. As mem- bers of the committee were appointed from the ;list of managers' if Mr. Roberts would like to be on the corn- mittee he for one should be very glad.—Mr. Roberts I No, sir, that is not my idea at all. I only want to have your opinion as to whether they as managers are worth retaining: that is all.—The Chairman said it was always thought desirable in an institution of that kind to have gentlemen in the town connected in some form or other with the bank, so that they can recom- mend people who were thrifty to deposit their money in the bank, and so help themselves.—Mr. Holman remark- ed that the managers could come at any time.—The CHAIRMAN said they could come at any time to see how the work was going on and alto give their advice when they found anything worth saying. It was very proper for several reasons that there should be 'managers of the bank.—Mr. R. Devil's said he did not think Messrs. Roberts and Fleming referred to that. They knew that under the old systemevery entry in the bank book was initialled by a manager, a practice which was given up. —The CILAIRMAN said it was given up because it was found difficult to get a manager to attend frequently. Last neat aw dreamt aw laid me deaun I' that owd snug at th' "Bull ,"I An' eh, By Gyow ! the comic things Ez rattlet throo my skull ! Aw thowt my chums wur rowlin' reawnd Me wile aw wur i' bed; Each cover.% wi' a horse cloth, an' A buzby on his yed I Fost, Birley Bill coom ragin' up; His cossin' war immense ; He'd just bin sittin' on a corpse, An miss'd his eighteenpence ! An' then owd Bashaw rowler't in, Wi' twenty bonny kids ; Two big shim rappits wi' red e'en, An' twothry Sammy Bride ! Th' Owd•Skoller, too, wur close bebint He look'd a gradely wag, Wi' his widow helpin' him to shift A goose an' green baize bag! A sojer follow'd, brandishin' A swippo, or a flail; At least, aw thowt so, but it proved A British lion's tail! Then suddenly aw seed blue fire, An' brimstone smel't eautside; Fer ".Cocker" hed bin fottin' up A forrin lookin' guide! Theer, too, at least a theausand imps Wur strugglin' to get in; But th' station mester wur abeaut, An' deyd soon stopt their din! Soon him an' " Robert" breausted off— Wi' voices rayther worn— " Christians awake! an' aw true men Salute this happy morn !" It made me Icwf till aw wur ill, An' wakkent wi' a scream; Wen lookin' reaund abeaut fer chums, Aw fund it wur a dream! So here mi rhymin' eends, an' Good luck to greyt an' smaw. Aw wish a Merrie Rrissmus, an' A Grand New Year to aw !

div.head: I GREAT COLLIERY FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: I GREAT COLLIERY FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
30 MEN ENTOMBED. RESCUE OF THE IMPERILLED MEN.

- About nine o'clock on Thursday night, information was received at St. Helens rown Hall that a great fire was raging at the Phcenix Colliery, belonging to Messrs. ;Glover, Urinson and Glover, at Sutton, St. Helens. Be- fore arriving at the place it was evident by the country around being illuminated that the report was only too true, and greatcrowds of people began to congregate in the neighbourhood, occupying every point of vantage which could be gained. When Superintendent Birchall, with the full strength of the Fire Brigade, steam engine, hose reel, and all appliances, arrived on the spot the fire had obtained a., firm whole of the headgear, including the brow cabins, platform and waggons. The greatest anxiety prevailed on account of there being a large num- ber of men, estimated at thirty or forty, in the pit As soon as the fire broke out it was impossible to raise the men, as the winding apparatus was rendered unsafe. The pit shaft is a very short one, and this, it was known, would have the effect of allowing the dense and suffo- cating smoke to get down the shaft to them very soon. In the initial stages of the fire the men were heard rantically shouting for help, but at this juncture none could be rendered to them. Word was passed to the men below to draw the brattice cloth across the pit eye, and thus prevent, as far as possible, Any of the suffocating smoke from reaching them. Communication with them was then stopped, and for the next hour nothing so far as could be ascertained, was heard, and great excitement prevailed as to the condition the men were in. At half-past ten the man- ager, Mr. Marsh, and five other men descended the pit to ascertain the position of affairs below. When the .knocks were given, a quarter of an hour later, to be wound up, there was breathless silence on the bank, and when two of the men who had gone down emerged from the cage they were eagerly asked if the men below were safe. The replies were vague and unsatisfactory, but at a later hour, although definite information was not obtainable, it was believed that the men below were all alive. The shaft is only 80 yards deep, but the workings extend a 'wig way. It is believed that the fire originated from a stove in the check-weightman's cabin on the pit brow. The head gear, though charred, was, on being tested a little later, found safe, and about half-past eleven the men were wound up two and four at a time, the pit being cleared about midnight. All were thankful for the miraculous escape.

div.head: GREAT CANAL MAKER ON HIS DEATHBED.
div.p: THE GREAT CANAL MAKER ON HIS DEATHBED.
A PATHETIC INCIDENT.

A domiciliary search was made on Sunday at Ches- naye, the country house of M. Ferdinand de Lesseps, but the fact was concealed from him. He is still alive, but, says the " Standard " correspondent, to all intents and purposes is no longer of this world. He cannot move without assistance, and has completely lost his memory. The same correspondent recalls a scene which occurred eight months ago, while he was lying ill in bed at ' his Paris residence in the Avenue Montaigne. A sum- mons arrived for him to appear before M. Prinet, the examining magistrate. The members of his family and a few faithful friends met in consultation, and de- cided to break the news to him as gently as possible. As soon as he understood the matter, M. de Lesseps rose in his bed and called for his clothes and his Grand Cordon of the Legion of Honour. Those who witnessed it say they will never forget the marvel they witnessed. The old man, who, but a few minutes before, had seemed too weak to move, got out of bed, dressed himself in haste, put on his Grand Cordon, and descended the stairs without any assist- ance. What took place at the interview between himself and M. Pripet is not known in all its details ; but M. de Lesseps defended not only his management of the Canal Company, but also the canal itself. The shock was, however, too much for him. He returned home, went to bed, and was seized with fever. The next day he said to his wife, "What a terrible nightmare I have, had I imagined I was summoned before the Examin- ing Magistrate ; it was atrocious." By degrees he be- came conscious that it was not a dream, and from that day he has never spoken of Panama.

div.head: PIT DISASTER AT WIGAN.
div.p: THE PIT DISASTER AT WIGAN.
FUNERALS OF VIOTIMS.
STRIKING INSTANCES OF BRAVERY.

WIGAN, SUNDAY NIGHT.—As the whole of the work- ings at Bamfurlong Colliery, near Wigan, the scene of the unfortunate fire last Wednesday, have now been fully examined by Mr. Hutchinson, manager, aud his staff, and as no one has been reported missing at the colliery offices, it is hoped that sixteen will be the total death roll. Sympathetic inqniries have been made by various bodies, one coming from the North Stafford- shire Miners Association, whilst the sad event was re- ferred to yesterday in many places of worship in the district. All the bodies were removed from the shed at the pit to their homes on Friday, and the interments took place on Saturday and yesterday. The manager attributes the saving of his life to the bravery of Dr. Webster. of Wigan, who found him 300 yards past the fire, and helped him out. The striking bravery of the under-manager, John Foster, forty years of age, has not been fully noticed. He himself dragged twelve men through the flames and smoke past the burning engine house. He was overcome and stricken down during his exertions, but was pulled out of danger by a fireman and another man. Foster saw other men ly- ing there, and these are supposed to have been those who were killed. This brave fellow is only now re- covering his eyesight, his eyes having been injured by the flames and fumes. Every praise is due to the doctors, under-managers, and neighbouring officials for their great efforts. Mr. Matthews, assistant inspector, was at the pit on Saturday, preparing plans for the coroner's inquiry.
GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS AND FAIR LABOUR.

A deputation from the Dublin Trades Council waited upon Mr. Morley, chief secretary, on Wednesday, for the purpose of gaining his support to the enforcement of the resolution of the House of Commons of February 13, 1891, with reference to Government contracts and fair labour. The proceedings were private. The deputa- tion included Messrs. Shelley, Simmons, Dowd, Richard- son, and Collins. They directed the attention of the Chief Secretary to the state of affairs at the Queen's Printing Office, giving the number of men and boys employed there respectively as 126 and 88. This, it was urged, was grossly disproportionate, and utterly against the spirit of the House of Commons resolution, which expressed the opinion that competent workmen only should be employed on Government contracts. Refer- ence was also made to the Educational Board, and the deputation said the resolution was not observed by that Board with respect to the Board of Works, the Prison Service, the Post-office, and other departments. Illus- trations were given to show that the resolution was a dead letter.—Mr. Morley, in reply, assured the deputa- tion of his thorough sympathy with the object they had in view. He promised that he would look into the matter, and would do all in his power to assist the workmen of Dublin.

div.head: LIBERATOR BUILDING SOCIETY
div.p: THE LIBERATOR BUILDING SOCIETY
COLLAPSE. POOR COMFORT FOR SHAREHOLDERS.

Another meeting of depositors of the Liberator Build- ing Society was held in London, on Tuesday. The Offi- cial Receiver (Mr. C. J. Stewart) said that in the report issued last January it was stated that interest at the rate of 5 per cent, had been earned on all the shares sub- scribed for previous to the 31st December, 1890, and 4 per cent, on later shares, and £5,000 was added to the reserve fund. The money, however, was provided by being borrowed at from 6 to 22 per cent, per annum. The ordinary building society business was insufficient by about £lO,OOO a year to pay the bare working ex- penses of the, staff. A committee was appointed to act with the liquidator. At a meeting of shareholders the Chairman said he could hold out but very slight hope of a dividend being paid to the shareholders. At both meetings there were cries of indignation at the absence of Mr. J. S. Balfour.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
THE NOMINATIONS.

Maitland Wood, The Vicarage, Higher Runcorn, by J. E. Meredith and Henry White ; also by William Whittaker and Alfred Buck; and also by William Banks and John Gatliffe. .

Those marked by an asterisk are members of the present Board. Mr. W. M. Sowerly, manager of Run- corn Alkali Works, was nominated, but through an informality the nomination was declared a " had one and rejected. REV. JOHN SIMPSON AND RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. In connection with the election, the Rev. John Simp- son preached a sermon on "Religious Education "in the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, to a large congregation. The preacher selected his text from 2 Tim. ii, 2. and in the course of his remarks said that education was essentially a religious question. Certain important points were being now brought forward, which all professing Christians should earnestly consider No sensible man could be indifferent when anything arose which endangered the thoroughness of education. The greatest enemy of religion was ignorance. So long as the people were educated and enlightened, it had then nothing to fear. But, unfortunately, there had always been a certain class that had hindered the progress of education. The spread of knowledge meant to this class the weakening of their power and authority. A little while ago the Bishop of Cnester took a journey down to the hamlet of Moulton with the sole object of persuading the people there to hand over their rights, with respect to the education of their children, into the ' hands of the clerical party. But the workingmen gave him their answer when they voted three to one for a School Board. Undaunted by this rebuff, his Lordship wrote to the people of Birkenhead, endeavouring to rob the parents of their right of free education. He who is the representative of the church that has ever striven to impede the march of religious liberty, even dared to speak of religious liberty. Then he further made a grave charge against the Board system, by saying that it undermined the religion of Jesus Christ. It all amounted to this, that the religion his Lordship would have taught in day schools should Ise only that which was calculated to make episcopalians. The important question was— Shall positive religious teaching be given in our day schools ? Then to any thoughtful person it was obvi- ously unjustto tax Nonconformists or Roman Catholics for the support of the teaching of the Church catechism. The beliefs of the different theological schools must go. The conscience of every child and parent must be res- pected. It was thought by a certain class that anybody and everybody was it to teach religion. There was nothing more dangerous than that, nothing which cal- culated more to foster insincerity and scepticism than a doctrine of that kind. They as Non- conformists had too great a reverence for the Gospel of their Lord to allow it to be taught in their 1 day schools by incompetent teachers. God knew they might have no religion to teach them. How in the world can a man lead a child to God who has never been to God himself? How could he know the way? The work of religious teaching must rest—not on the State, but in the Church, and in the parents of the children. The State could never teach religion until they could prove that the State was a thoroughly and wholly religious one. A great responsibility was placed upon the shoulders of parents—who had to see to it that the religious education of their children was only com- mitted to faithful men. As Christian citizens it was their religious duty that they put in authority only those men who should strive to give the children of the very poorest the best education they were capable of receiv- ing. They must see to it that they were not actuated by mere sectarian spirit, but by the pure desire to give them that which should lift them into greater comfort, strengthen them in temptation, and make real men and women of them—men and women after Christ's heart.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The ordinary monthly meeting of the Widnes School Board was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. There were present :—Mr. H. Wade Deacon, C.C. in the chair), Dean Finegan, Revs. J. H. Garrett, Father Clarke. Dr. 0' Reeffe and Messrs. C. Flynn, S. Quinn, C. E. Barlow, B. Brown, B. Shaw, D. Lewis, and G. H. Danby clerk.
PROSECUTIONS AND GRANTS.

The district Education Committee reported that dur- ing the month of November (3 weeks) 17 applications for papnent of fees were granted, and out of 27 prosecu- tions 26 convictions had been obtained.

The School Management Committee submitted their annual report, which showed that the grants earned per child in average attendance at Simm's Cross School was 19s. 6did. against 20s. lid. last year, a decrease of aid. ; at Warrington-road School, 19s. std.,against 18s. 7d., an increase of 100. ; at West Bank School, 19s. sp., against 19s. 7d., a decrease of lid. ; the average grant of the three schools was 20s. Oid. against 20s. ltd. last year, a decrease of id. The total grant this year amounted to £2,893 95., against £2,844 Os. 6d. last year, while the average attendance was 2,825 this year, against 2,774.—The Rev. Dean Finegan moved the adop- tion of this report, and said that it was, when taken into consideration all round, a very satisfactory report, and reflected great credit upon the teachers.—The re- port was unanimously adopted, and the Committee were thanked for preparing it.

div.head: TIIII REMISSION OF FEES.
div.p: TIIII REMISSION OF FEES.

Mr. D. Lewis then moved the following motion : "That, inasmuch as by the Elementary Education Act, 1.891., the right to the education of their children without payment of fees is conferred upon all parents who desire it, applications for the payment of fees on the ground of poverty should net be heard by the District Education Committee." He made the motion, he said, owing to the fact that the District Education Committee undo, the existing regulations of the board had to hear applica- tions for the remission of school fees on the ground of the poverty of the applicant. During the time that he (Mr. Lewis) had at on the committee a number of such applications had been made, and there was no doubt that the committee had the power under the Act of Parliament of 1870 to perform the unpleasant function of inquiring into the means of those requiring free places in the schools. On the other hand, however, under the provisions of the Education Act of last year the exercising of this authority was rendered superfluous land unnecessary, it being distinctly stated in one of the 'sections that any parent either in England or Wales, irrespective of his or her means, was entitled to free Iplaces in elementary schools. Such being the case, it was plainly unnecessary that parents should have to go through the ordeal of having an inquiry made into their ability or otherwise to contribute some small payment towards their children's education: He maintained that since the passing of the Free Education Act of last year the committee had no power to enforce the payment of fees, and hence the inquiries of the committee were reduced to a farce.—Mr. B. Brown seconded the motion and the Rev. Dean Finegan opposed it, remarking that he considered it was quite unnecessary to take such a step until the time arrived when the difficulty compelled them. He contended that if the motion were passed it would only increase the present heavy School Board rate. Another thing, he considered that the motion was of a revolutionary character, and was in- tended in a revolutionary spirit.—The Rev.G. IT Garrett did not see much necessity for the resolution, and he considered that the people of Widnes were sufficiently independent to subscribe the small sum asked for to- wards the education of their children.—The Rev. Father Clarke said that as a matter of fact parents had not to appear before the Education Committee to state their circumstances. Application was made to the teacher at a school, and a note was then sent down to their clerk, who brought the matter before them.—The Chairman suggested that the matter be referred to the District Education Committee, and thoroughly thrashed out by them. After further discussion, Mr. Lewis consented to withdraw his motion, on the understanding that he should bring it forward at the next meeting of the Dis- trict Education C.immittee.
