WOMEN AS RELIEVING OFFICERS.

Mr. Fowler and Sir Walter Foster may be heartily con- gratulated (says the "Daily Chronicle ") on a little piece of administrative reform to which they have just set their hand. This is the appointment of a woman as a relieving officer—the very first of her kind. The appoint- ment is for a Warwickshire district, and has caused a good deal of local enthusiasm. There seems to have been no reason—save sheer conservatism and indifference— why a similar step was not taken before, especially as women are in some respects rather better fitted for the I work than a good many men.

div.head: TTTE " DA.RKEST ENGLAND" SCHEME.
div.p: TTTE " DA.RKEST ENGLAND" SCHEME.

REPORT OF THE INVESTIGATING COMMITTEE The report of Lord Onslow's Committee on the ad- ministration of the" Darkest England" scheme of the Salvation Army is publislitd. It states that the subscrip- tions and donotions from the public up to the 30th of September, amounted to £129,288. Consideration is. given chiefly to the farm colony, asto which the Com- mittee state that there is no evidence of any waste of money, and that they are of opinion that every reason- able offer has been made to secure success. The working to the present time exhibits a loss, but it would be un- fair to judge the institution by one year's working. There is no reason to think that General Booth or any member of his family derives, or ever has derived bene- fit of any kind from any of the properties or monies re- ceived from the Darkest England" scheme. Some members of General Booth's family draw salaries from the spiritual wing of the Salvation Army. A list was furnished from which it appears that, General Booth himself has received nothing from. either side of the Salvation Army. He has a small income, partly settled on him by a friend and partly derived from the sale of his works, the amount and nature of which he explained to the Committee,and which seemed to them commensurate with the mainten- ance of his personal establishment. It appears to the Committee that the subscribers to the fund intended to invest General Booth with an unlimited discretion in the disposal of the sums subscribed if exercised within the area of the objects set out in the appeal made to the public, and the manner of the application to the funds to the purposes contemplated must be left to the deter- mination of the General of the Salvation Army for the time being. But while it seems necessary that the floating and current cash should be at the absolute dis- posal of that officer, and whilst it would have been in- expedient to interfere with the exercise of his discretion when dealing in accordance with the terms of the deed poll with the real property and investments, yet it is desirable, the Committee think, that the two lest-named classes of property should be held in the name of inde- pendent trustees.

The " Darkest TIIE report of the Committee England" which was formed for the purpose lnvistigation, of inquiring into the administra- tion of the "In Darkest England "fund has been published this week. It is to all intents and pur- poses, a complete vindication of General Booni against the aspersions and insinuations which have been levelled against him, 30 far, at all events, as these were taken cognisance of by the Committee. With regard to the composition of the Committee itself little exception could be taken. It origi- nally consisted of the Earl of ONsLow, Sir H. JAMES, M.P., Mr. SYDNEY BUXTON", M.P., Mr, WALTER BONG, and Mr. EDWIN WATERHOUSE, president of the Institute of Chartered Account- ants ; and Mr. C. Honitorsn, M.P., as hon. secre- tary. Mr. SYDNEY BTJXTON had, however, in consequence of a severe domestic bereavement to resign his position on the Committee. Eight- een meetings had been held and twenty- nine witnesses examined. The Committee testify that they have received the fullest aesit. tance from the officers of the Salvation Army, and that every opportunity was given to those who had charges to prefer against the "General" or his subordinates, to tender evidence. The Com- mittee's investigations were exclusively devoted, in the first place, to ascertaining whether the moneys collected in connection with the "Darkest England" scheme had been devoted to the objects and been expended in the methods set out in the appeal. In the second place, inquiry was made as to whether the money was being spent in a business-like and prudent manner; and, under the third and last leading the Committee sought to ascertain whether the "Darkest Englandlund was a: safeguarded as to prevent its misapplication either now or after the death of General Boom Under the first and second of these " counts " the verdict, if we may use the word, of the ,Commit- tee may be said to be unequivocally in favour of the Salvation Army, so far, of course, as the pro- gress of the scheme would allow of a definite judg- ment being arrived at. With regard to the third "count," the Committee, while of the opinion that the invested property resulting from the appeal is so vested and controlled by the trust of the deed of January 30, 1891, that any application of it to purposes other than those declared in the "Deed" by any General of the Salvation Army, would amount to a breach of trust and would sub- ject him to proceedings of a civil or criminal character, yet adequate legal safegoards do not at present exist to prevent the misapplication of the property. Therefore, in addition to some minor suggestions, the Committee recommend that the real property holdings and the investments in stocks should be held in the names of indepen- dent trustees. Another suggestion of the Com- mittee is a significant one when we take into account some of the charges that have been made against " Army" methods. It is " that every care should be taken when disposing of the articles produced in the institutions under the control of the social wing, that the prices charged should not be lower than those which may fairly be demanded by ordinary tradesmen or work- men." In connection with this it is satisfactory to note that "Mr. BOOTII has earnestly assured the committee that he will never undersell the ordinary trade iu any commodity made at his

"factories." There are in great towns many small industries—. wood-chopping for example the workers in which are barely able to make a living by their own efforts, .and it would be in the highest degree unfortunate if these workers were forced, by the competition of the "Darkest England factories into the ranks of the unemployed. A good deal of criticism has been directed against the operations of General BOOTH'S scheme on this ground alone, and it would, in some respects, have been satisfactory if the investigating -eommittee had been able to pronounce an opinion as to the validity of these criticisms. That, how- ever, scarcely came within the scope of their inquiry. In the matter of the personal expenses -of the BOOTH famify the report of the Committee is conclusive. It required a singular obtuseness or an abnormal development of malice to accuse General BOOTH of a desire to accumulate personal . wealth. Whatever may be said of his ambitions -or weaknesses in other directions, the whole tenour of his life goes to shpw that he is not a " money- grabber "of the vulgar type. In matters of this kind there is absolutely no ground for comparison between General BOOTH and, say, the late little- lamented JAI' GOULD. Yet insinuations of a more or less vague and general, but none the less injurious, character have from time to time been made as to the manner in which the funds Of the Salvation 'Army and the "Darkest England" scheme were expended. On this point the Committee speaks out with per- fect clearness. "There is no reason to think," they report, "that Mr. Boors or any Member of his family derive, or ever have derived, benefit of any 'kind from any of the properties or money raised for the "Darkest England" Scheme. Some members of Mr. Boorn's family draw salaries ' from the spiritual wing of the Salvation Army, and a list was put in from which it appears that Mr. BOOTH himself has received nothing from either side of the Salvation Army. He has a small income partly settled on him by a personal friend and partly derived from the sale of his literary 'works, the amount and nature of which he ex- plained to the Committee, and which seemed to them commensurate with the maintenance of his personal establishment." The appointment of the Vommittee of Inquiry was to a great extent prompted by those who have consistently dispar- aged General BOOTH and his works, and to those who have anticipated that its investigations would result in sensational disclosures of gross misman- agement, even if not of dishonest malversatien, the actual report must have brought a keen disappoint- ment. There are few" schemes "of anything like the same complexity, and presenting so many possibilities of honest error, which could have come oat of such an inquiry as scatheless, even though they had been couducted on the strictest "com- mercial principles."

"Dr. NANSEN, the famous arctic explorer, has thrown his testimony on the side of those who argue that such stimulants as alcohol and tobacco lessen the physical endurance of the people who indulge in them. Dr. NANSEN is himself a stal- wart Norwegian who has amply proved that he possesses both physical and mental qualities of more than an average kind. His crossing of 'Greenland was a feat that required an indomit- able spirit and a body capable of the utmost en- durance. He and his six companion a traversed a distance of between four and five hundred miles 'on foot, dragging along with them hand sledges •oontaining clothing and provisions sufficient for a protracted journey. They had to fight against blinding snowstorms, to scale mountains of ice, and to face an intensely void and biting wind. Dr. NANSEN'S experii and observation on the journey convinced him that stimulants are the reverse of helpful when regular and steady work is required. As to tobacco, while conceding that it is less destructive than alcohol, it has, be says, not only an injurious influence on 'the digestion, but .it lessons the strength of the body and reduces nervous power, capacity for en- durance, and tenacity of purpose. He does not think it advisable that, excessive smokers or 'chewers of tobacco should attempt anything so arduous and trying as Arctic exploration. In pre- paring for his projected voyage to the North Pole, Dr. NANSEN will no doubt act up to his opinion in selecting his crew, and it will certainly be some- thing for the anti-s.nokers to boast about, if a crew of non-smokers are the first to come back and tell us all about the Pole.

A PROPOSAL was made at a meeting of Widnes School Board on Tuesday, which was so uniro- peach:ll)ly reasonable that one might have con- eluded beforehand that it would be adopted, as some reporters say, nem. con. Yet it was:rejected, or, if not quite rejected, it was unmistakably " shelved " by being referred to a Committee. The proposal was to the effect that " as by the Ele- mentary Education Act, 1891, the right to the education of their children without payment of fees is conferred upon all parents who desire it, applications for the payment of fees on the ground of poverty should not be heard by the District Education Committee." The intention of the mover of this resolution was evidently to bring the regulatiGns of the School Board into harmony with the new state of things created by the recent Education Act. For why :shculd parents be either expected or asked to apply to any committee for the remission of school fees on the ground of their poverty, when they can demand free education for their children as a legal right? Notwithstanding this, there " were no fewer than three clerical gentlemen who spoke against the harmless necessary proposition, and one of them, the Rev. Dean FINEGAN, con- sidered it was quite revolutionary in its character. If there be anything revolutionary in the new departure in educational matters, it ought to be some consolation to Dean FINEGAN to know that the fires of revolution were lit so far back as 1891, when the Education Act was passed by the late 'Tory Government, and that they have long since burned themselves out. All that is now needed is a little evolution to bring the methods of the school Board into accordance with education law as it now is.

OVERILEAD V. UNDERGROUND TELEPHONES. At a meeting of the St. Helens Paving Committee on Wednesday, an application from the Liverpool Corporation for permission to erect ten poles along the Rivington pipe-line from the Toll Bar to the borough boundary was read. It was stated that the Liverpool Corporation proposed erecting a telephone from Liverpool to Rivington.—The Borough Sur- 'Yeyor thought the wires should be put underground and thought it time that the National Telephone Company, whose trunk wires in St. Helens are overhead, should put them underground.—lt was decided that permission should be given, subject to the Liverpool Corporation removing the poles if required by the St. Helens Cor- poration, and notice was given of the in- tention of the St. Helens Corporation to have in the near future all telephone wires under- ground. A SUSPECTED POACHER AT RUNCOILL • John Davies, Stone Croft, Halton-road, Runcorn, was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, for coming from land where he was supposed to have been in search of game, and with having in his posses- sion a net used for taking game, on the .7.l)th inst. About midnight on the date in question P.C.'s Fryer and Royle were passing the gas tank in Halton-road when they saw the defendant, who was in a hurry. They noticed something under his army and. he refusing to say what it was, they took from him the net produced.. He de- clined to give any explanation. He was violent, and they had to put him en the ground to gain possession of the net.—Defendant denied that that he was coming from land. He got the net from a navvy, to fenc,e off son:e fowls.—Fined ss. and costs, and, it was decided that the net should be destroyed. Its dimensions are 69ft. long, 15ft. 3m. width of beam, and 81t.61n.depth of hold,and it is registered to carry 160 tons in deep water. Built of the best rock elm, English oak, and pitch-pine, she contains all recent improvements, and is the largest fiat built on the bankao£ the Bridge- water Canal. RUNCORN SONS OH TRMPHRANCII. 1 A meeting was held in connection with this society on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas fleeson. There was a large attendance. •Mr.J. Somerville read a paper on Local Option. In the course of it condemned in in strop.' terms the present system of licens- ing which is in the hands of the magistrates. Ile spoke. of the many evils arising from intemperate habits, and the great amount of misery caused by alcoholic drink& Ile dilated upon the necessity of their insisting upon. the ratepayers having the supreme power, with regard to the granting: of licensing. They ought to have the direct veto in those matters. Whatever measures of temperance reform were passed ought to be the genuine article. An animated discussion ensued in which Messrs. Edward Key, John Jones, David Smith. Thomas S. Bolt, George E. Sutton, Thomas Cooke, Daniel Bisbrown, and S. M. Timperley took part. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Somerville for his excellent paper. JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladies' silver and gold watches in the town.—Advt. RECHABITES AT RUNCORN. After tea, the tent, which is conducted by the boys themselves, with their President, vice-President, trm, was opened in due form, and a number of candidates were initiated. There were short addresses delivered by Bros. Rev. J. P. Williams, Robert Evans, D.C.R., J. E. Warburton, D.S., James Lea, D.T., James Richardson, T.S., and J. Sayle, J.S. Recitations were also given by Bios, J. J. Oliver, T. Lawson, N. MacLeod, G. A. Warbuiton J. Howard and E. Gatley, also a quartet by Bros. W. S. flarrop, T. Baxter, J. J. Oliver and W. Oliver. Bro. W. Cartwright, P.C.R., presented each member with a copy of the "Juvenile Rochabite " for December, in which appears an excellent photograph of himself, with a short sketch of his temperance career. Fruit was also distributed during the evening, and the meet ing, which was much enjoyed, was then closed by the President, Bro, T. Sayle, ' with the usual ceremonies.

The usual monthly meeting of the Free Library COM- mittee was hell in the Free Library,on Wednesday,under the chairmanship of Mr. Thomas Riley. The Librarian reported that 2,063 works had been issued during the month of INoYember, being an increase of 263 on the corresponding month last year. A list of books contain- ing 159 vols.of books of an interesting and useful charac- ter was passed, and recommended to be , purchased. Accounts amounting to 18s. 9j. were passed tor payment. The minute passed at the last meeting recom- mending that the library be opened on Wednes- day afternoon from 2 to 4. was sent back to the Committee from the Ito.ird of Commissioners with a view to considering the advisability of granting extended facilities to the public, by opening! the Library on other evenings in addition to those obtainirn, at present. It was therefore recommended that the Library be openeckevery evening in the week except Friday from 6 o'clock to 8, and on each Wednesday and Saturday afternoomfrom 2 to 4,and that the salary of the librarian be increased £lO per annum to commence January sth, 1863. Beyond the extra smartness imparted to their estab- lishments by the tradesmen, there is little to indicate .that Christmas is 'so near at hand. The condition of the Widnes atmosphere is of such quality that window displaya are not at any time of great magnitude, the gases working havoc amongst the fabrics,,&c..exhibited, and there is nothing of a novel character now to be seen.. The embellishment are confined to sprigs of holly and mistletoe and brightly-coloured ribbons, and paper. It is to be feared that the Christmastide wBl not be a very merry one to many of the working population. The I7nited Alkali Company have -ordered that the plant for the manufacture of caustic soda must he stopped for an indefinite period ,and this perind,it is said. will, wrtainly extend to six weeks. The suspension is to take effect ii the 28th inst., and upwards of 1,000 men will be thrown idle in Widnes. The prospect for the•families who will thus be adversely aftstted is not a ver.r. bright one, and we regret to thinlg.that in many instances the pinch of want will be felt. The people of liurizeru are more fortunate from a trade-point of view. The-Manchester Ship Canal Works have prevented any scarcity of employment for some years pakt,and.hesides, the chemical trade is pretty brisk at present. V2TROLEUM STOVES.—GARLLND, Brldge-a.ireet. div.p: ST. HELEzeS__CORPORAVIaisiI AND NEW POWERS:

The new bill which has lust been prepared by St. Helens Corporation and deposited in the Hill Office of the House of Commons contains SOMA* im- portant clauses affecting property owners arid eon- tractors. No new street in...ending to have n oon- tinuous line of buildings shall, unless the Corpora- tion allow, be kid oat of more than 150/yards in length without an intersecting street. .ntrances to streets must be of equal width with the street. The Corporation may define the future line of streets, and may repair streets and fence vacant lands, and charge the cost to the owners. They shall have power to prohibit the construction of cellars in any part of the borough liahle to flood. In future every newly-constructed sewer shall have lat the higher eud a ventilating shaft. Powers are sought to extinguish all rights of berbage and all other commonable rights over Thatto Heath, Powers are also sought to deal more stringently in the matter of .sanitary arrangements, the isolation of persons suffering from infectious disease. Prin- cipals of school to furnish lists of pupils, suffering from infectious disease, &c. Many of the clauses refer to the creation of St. Helens Corporation re- deemable stock and the establishment of a couvsli- dated loans fund.

Webster (clerk), H. Gawthorpe (schoolmaster). The minutes of the previous meetings were read and confirmed. The correspondence of the months of November and December was read and considered. Ex-P. T. Albert Hewitt was appointed assistant master as from November Ist last. Accounts to the amount of £7O 14s. id. were passed for payment, and it was resolved to have the playground re-cmu dered. Tlre clerk reported he had received an application for Vie use of the school on the 29th i fist, for the purpose of holding a tee party and ball to raise funds to pay Mr.lhomas Howard, the late clvirchwarden, of St. Michael's Church, the amount owing to him .for sums advanced and expended by him in the church during his year of office, and which hitherto had not been paid to him ; and that as there was not a quorum, at the November meet- ing he (the clerk) had granted permission for the room to be used on the terms of resolution 102, and it was resolved that considering the special circum- stances of the case no charge be made for the use of the school on this occasion. SUMER OF A COACHMAN AT NEWTON. On Friday morning, a suicide of a painful nature occurred at Newton lake. Thomas W I liams,42 years of age,of 21,E1m-view,Latchford, coachman,had been out of employment for about six week and had in consequence been very despondent. lie came to Diewton on Thursday night, with his wife, on a visit to his brother-in-law, Mr. T. Pilling, of 23, High-st. He stayed there during the night, and it was his intention to proceed to Liverpool next day to meet a gentleman with reference to a situation. He had been low-spiriteil and despondent for some time, and suffered from sleeplessness for the last month, owing to disappointment and being out of work. At nine o'clock, his wife took him a cup ot tea upstairs. Lut he was unable to partake of it,and he afterwards got up and indulged in a smoke, lie then told his wife he would go and get a shave. On leaving the barber's shop, he was seen by his brother-in-law to go in the direction of the lake. Pilling told MT& Williams that he had seen her husband go in•the direction oB the lake, and she at ones followed him.and found is coat aid hat lying •on the landing stage. She,at once gave information to the police, who, after dragging with grappling irons, an hour-and-a-half, recovered the body 12 •yards from the bank, in 15 feet of water. An in- 'quest was held at the Blue &Al' lan,Newtori, by Mr. S. Brighouse, on Saturday, whoa evidence hearing out the above facts was' given by Mrs. Williams and Mr. Pilling, and a verdict a Suicide whilst temporarily insane" was returned.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND MEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND MEN AT
_ RUNCORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESDANDENT.

A boon and a blessing to readers of the popular three volume novels—and their name is legion—and to students of science history,anu general literature, will be the improved facilities proposed to be afforded to borrowers of books by the Runcorn Free Library Committee. It has long been felt that the hours during which the Library has been open have been altogether inadequate,besides being some- what inconvenient, andthere is no doubt the Board of Commissioners will ratify the new arrange- ment.

I have just heard of an amusing,' incident which occurred at a recent Meeting ot, ratepayers at Helsby with respect to the provision of a water supply for that rapidly increasing rural community. A gentleman described the water from a number ot wells in the locality as unlit for'human consump- tion, and very likely to cause disease, when a well known individual of burly proportions remarked " Pre lived here for seventy year sy and id doesn'd seem to hey' done me much harna47nnd added that it was only the people who came-from Widnes who complained. " Ah,' ahouted a voice from the audi- ence." an they're hauf jed when' they come." As a Widnes gentleman, in the person of Mr. James I White, was in the chair, and there were other Widuesians in the roorn,there were roars of laughter.

Preparations are being made-for the aged persont: treat, one of the most popular gatherings held in Runcorn during the year. Thursday,January 19th, has been fixed for the festival; by the Committee, who have also decided that. a " hot pot" dinner shall be provided, with tarts,. , and tea and coffee, and it is highly probable that Professor Miller. a Runcornian, who has made a reputation as an entertainer,will he engaged to amuse the old people. There will also be- scngs, humorous, and sentimental, and perhaps a few speeches by way of ballast. The secretaries have received several sub- ' stantial subscriptions from gentlemen residing out- side the town, and they are at-liberty and anxious to receive many more, and iv is to be hoped they will be forthcoming, for the worthy object of brightenitigjor a few hours, the sadly humdrum existence et too many of our aged poor. The donations received included .t..t2s. from Dr. Steele, Frodsham ; Lils. from Mr. George Whitley, con- servative candidate for the Northwich Division at the General Election ; Messrs. P. Walker and Co., and Messes. Greenall Whitley and Co., brewers; and £1 from Mr. Joseph Yerdin, J.P., D.L., of Northwioh.

The first public distribution of prizes to the children of Runcorn Board Schools was a most unqualified success. The only regrettable circum- stance. was the absence of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., through illness. The large ball was packed to suffocation, and the young people and their elders enjeoyed to the full the entertainment provided by a number of the scholars, which was highly credit- able to themselves mad to the teachers. Looking from the platform,,there was presented one sea of faces, and the way in which the young- ,sters relponded in their shrill trebles to the call of Canon Wood for three cheers fin- Mrs. Brunner appeared highly gratifying to that lady. Whest it was remembered wllat an up- Mll fight these schools had in the first two years ;of their existenae, their present high position as an • educational institution ie, not only surprising, but, tis a splendid testimony to the ea.:Macy of the staff.

On all hands regret is expressed at the untimely death of I%lns. W. W. Gossage, w'afes of Councillor Oossage, hf Widnes, from that, dreadful :,courge, typhoid lesion Both the people of Widnes and Runcorn have a sad interest. in the untoward event. The decsased lady, who was thsecond daughter of Mr. Arthur Keen, of Birmingham, was the sister of Major Harlehurst, of the latser place. Councillor, Gossage is also suffering from the same malady and lies in a somewhat critical condition at his father'S residence, Camp IIiJI, Woolton, whither he was removed immediately. after his wite'sdeath. Three daysTreviously, on Wednesday last weelr.an affecting scene took plaoa., Mr. Gossage was carried into the bedroom to bid hiq dying wife" good-bye" but she was then unconecious.and she continued in • that state until her death. The deceased lady was only thirty years of age, and the blow to her rela- tives may be somewhat chastened by the universal sympathy accorded to them.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CORPS.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CORPS.
DISTRIBUTION_ OP_ PRIZ

The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connection with the P and G (Runcorn) Companies of the 2nd C.H.Y. was held in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening. The audience was not of very large proportions. The officers present were Cap- tains 1.). Ashton. G. F. Ashton, Harrison (Frodaham), , Swift (Chester), the Rev. Dr. ,Preston, Chaplain, I.ieut. Speakman, Drill-Instructor Pia) et-. Quartermaster Ilankinsou, Colour-Sergeant Poole and Sergeants Joynson, Edwards, Woodland, Williams, Platt, Lee, and Harvey. , Captain D. Astrbm said he was sorry it had fallen to his lot to distribute the prizes of his own detachment. Mrs. C. W. Ilazlehorat had promised to do so, but Mrs. Gossage, her sister,, had died of typhoid fever,and conse- quently she was unable to fulfil her promise. Alluding to the detachment, Capiain Ashton said he was glad to say there was an improvement all round. Last year the detachment was 140 strong; this year it was 181; a gain of 21 men. Musketry had improved by seven per cent ; they had got nine more marksmen than last year ; and attendance at drill had considerably increased. raking it all round the detachment was very much better ; and they hoped for still further improvement in the conning season. It had been found necessary to make an altera- tion in their band.Mr.Outhwaite being the head-master, and he was more than satisfied with the result. (Applause.) Captain Ashton then distributed the pris.+ and afterwards he proposed a vote of thanes to the donors. They werer dependent upon the public to provide the funds for the twizes, and they had always found the public willing to aid them. Applause.) —Dr. Preston seconded the motion, and in the course of his remarks, he said recruits were intended to make the detachment much stronger than it was. He had it on authority that if it were not for the Volunteer force the hated system of conscription in force on ths con- tinent would be introduced, and young men would be compelled to serve in the militia. The war authorities, and those who could smells battle afar off, thought the day was not far distant when England would he com- pelled to go into war. Russia was on She move, and very soon perhaps England would have a life and death struggle with her for the retention of fndia, and then would devolve upon the Volunteers thedefence of hearth and home. As a matter of pa triotism,, it was the duty of every young man to enrol himself in the Volunteer force, and lie hoped that betore the next company met, there would be a great accession of strength to the Run- corn detachment, He congratulated Coronet Ashton and Captain Woolley upon the decoration they had obtained from the War Auttiorkies, and expressed, the hope that services of non-commissioned officers would be recog- nised in a somewhat similar manner. (Applause.) In conclusion he drew attention to the advantages for social intercourse and recreation afforded by the Volun- teer Social Club, and urged the volunteem present to join.—The motion was carried by acclamation. The following programme was then gone through :—March de Concert, the band ; selection, " Zkr Irnd Zimmer- mann," the band : duet, "Love and war," Messrs. James Lewis and Walter Limond ; song," Love's golden dream," Miss Janet Gardner ; pianofinte solo. " Last rose of summer," Mrs. Latimer, A.C.O. ;song. "Mona," Mr. James Lewia ; humorous song' Mr. Arthur Limond ; selection." La Reve D'or," the band ; trio, "Turn MI old time„' Miss Lewis, Messrs. Lewis and liimond ; cor- net solo, " Daughter of the Regiment," Mr. R. W. Pier- point; song, " Sunshine and rain," Miss Lewis 'song, • Soldier Jim," Mr. Walter Limond ;: humorous snug. Mr. Arthur Limond. Mrs. Latimer was the accompan- ist.

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIP-CUIT.
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIP-CUIT.
SALE OF WORK AND CHRISTMAS TREE.

With the object of raising funds for the repairing and refurnishing of the residence of the Superin- tendent 1119inister—Wesley Villa in tdreenway-rd.,---- . and for other circuit pairposes, a sale of work and Christmas tree were held in Brunswick school on Tuesday and Wednesday. The room had been decorated with a combkiation of pale blue and orange coloured material in a most tasteful cind effective manner, . by Mr., Eaton Speakman,and the stalls displayed a large variety of articles most attractively arranged. Th.) mem- bers of the sewing moeting,who had been most earnest and untiring in their labours tor the cause had a stall well stocked with useful), ornamental., and valuable goods, and the ladies in charge were: Mrs. Speakman, Mrs. Rushton, Mrs. Melkor, assisted by Mrs. Arrowsmith, Mrs. Hanby, Mrs..F. J. Norman, Mrs. A. R. Norman, Mrs. E. TaylorpMrs. Wilkes, Miss Gamon, Miss Percival Miss Rushton, Miss Speakman. The Christmas tree was heavily laden with'multifarious alck-nacks and *fine array of dolls,and in attendance were Miss Norman,Mi:s Janet Taylor, Miss Dobsomassistecl by Miss Andersom, Miss Crosby, Miss B. Rowland, Miss Simister, Miss Simkin, Miss Spearing, Miss Alice Taylor, Miss Unswo.sth, Miss Williams, Mies Wiswall. The good things of the refreshment stall,which needed no recommendation to visitors, were dispensed by Mrs. Sowerby„ Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Dykos, assisted by Mrs. Dyer, Mrs..Grahain, :ers. J. D. Jones, Mrs. Lea,th wood, Mrs.Leoouteur,Miss M.Croshy,Zvliss I.Crosby,Miss Jones, Miss A....lones,Miss Massey,Miss Howland. There was also a fish pond,in charge of Miss Wisveall,and a Bran pie, in care of Misses Nellie Lowe, Alice Lowe, and May Bellamy. There was a good attendance at the opening ceremony which was performed by Mr. Alderman Mc Kechine, of St. Helens. Amongst those noted were the Revs. T. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmith, and J. Hanley, j Messrs. E. Speakman, F. J. Norman' A. R. Norman, A. , Harrison, Win. Sowerby, &Pope J. D. Junes, T. Simis- ter, J. Taylor, 'l'. Boote, J. Mtivueaux, J. Simpson, J. ' M Frith,k. Morris, J. Povah, E. Marshall, T. Cooke, G. Bellamy, J. Leadstoae, and J. D. Jones. Mr. Wilkes

conducted the proceedings, Mr. Hanley read a psalm, and Mr. Arrowsmith offered up prayer. In explaining the objects for which the bazaar was held the Rev. Thomas Wilkes mentioned that in the circuit there were three married ministers, which meant that there were three houses to be kept up by an income from 1 various sources. One of the houses, that in Greenway- road, belonged to the circuit, the others they paid rent for. In the latter houses they expected the landlords to do t'ae repairs, but in their own house they had to bear the expense et repairs. Nine months aga it became an absolute necessity that some repairs should be done, and they were done in part, but the roof required to be im- mediately attended to as the rain was penetrating now in three places. The ladies had taken the matter in hand, and instead of that sale being the small affair it was at first contemplated it had assumed proportions none of them ever dreamt of. He had never been asso- ciated with a nobler band of Christian workers than be had been on that occasion. (Applause.) Alderman McKechnie expressed the pleasure he felt in being present, and his admiration at the tasteful decors- ' tion of the room. The ladies deserved the very greatest credit for the way in which they had stocked the stalls, and displayed their beautiful wares. He trusted the sale of work would be a great success and that they would be able to carry out their splendid idea of refur- nishing and repairing the minister's house. (Applause.) He then formally declared the baz tar open, and the ladies at once commenced busiuess.—Alderman McKechnie besides giving a donation of LIO to the sewing meeting stall, made numerous purchases.

_ On Wednesday, the second day, the proceedings were opened by Mr. *John Sitnpson. After the usual devo- tiemal exercises in which the Rev. T. Wilkes, and the Rev. R. Possnett took part, Mr. Simpson delivered a speech in which he recalled the time, sixty-four years ago, when the building in which they were assembled was erected in the midst of fields. A few years after- wards, someone who had not much regard for Wesleyan Methodism, but simply thought about his own pocket built the cottages opposite without back doors, and this altered the character of the neighbourhood. He re- counted the various houses the circuit had possessed for their minister, and referring to the present one in Greenway-road said it required repairing and refurnish- ing, and had it not been for the ladies sewing meeting volunteering their services to raise the money, he did not know what they should have done, lie was glad to be assocatecl with this bazaar because in the first place it was for a good cause, secondly because it had been taken up and carried on with such heartiness and good feeling, and thirdly because of the large amount of hearty support they had receive* from their friends. The first day was a greater success than any of them dared to hope for, upwards of £l2O tieing raised and he attributed a great deal of this success to Alderman McKechnie, whom be described as a liberal min led,open handed man. He hoped the success would be continued that afternoon and evening.

The entertainment given each evening was a great source of attraction, and included magic lantern exhibi- tions, Romberg's " Toy Symphony," miscellaneous con- certs, speaking bees, palmistry, and receptions by Father Christmas. The sum realised in the two days amounted to £2lO.

div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAItD ELECTION 3
MEETING OF CANDIDATE 3.
EXTRAORDINA RT PROCEEDINGS.-AN_ ELECTION AVOIDED.

At the invitation of Mr. James Pritchard, chairman of Runcorn School Board, a meeting of candidates and their nominators was held on Thursday night in the Commissioners' Board-room. Mr. Pritchard presided, and there were present Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. J. Pul- ford Williams. Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, J. M. Frith, ,L K. Diggs, W. Ha nkinssn, E. W. Humphreys, J. R. Frith, John Brundrit, J.P., T. Bowyer, J Meadow- croft, J. Gatley, B. Kitiveton, J. Gates, G. Moss. F. Oliver, D. Bisbrown, F. J. Nonatan, A. IL Norman, E. Imison, S. Pearson, T. Lea, W. Banks, H. Coleburo, A. Salkeld, E. Gregory, C. A. Timmins, S. Pope, J. H. Weston, John Weston, J. Holt, J. Clarke, Jos. Pritchard. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman said he was not aware that the policy of the Board had teen to any ' extent questioned, and if it had been the members could show good educational results. The Board had taken advantage of every recent Act of Parliament to promote educational objects. The better plan would he, therefore, to at once proceed to see if some arrangement could be made as far as possible to avoid the expense and turmoil of a contested election partioularly at Christmas titne.—Mr. Frith said all the old members were nominated ; did they intend to stand He understood that Mr. Salkeld retired in favour of Mr. Imision.—Mr. Salkeld : That is so.—Mr. Imison : I think Mr. Salkeld retires—not in favour of anyone.—A long pause took place, which called forth the remark trnm the Chairman that as none of the candidates ! appeared willing to withdraw, and meeting' would be ! fruitless.—Mr. Meedowcroft said he objected to the proposal of the Board to extinguish private schools in the I town, which he described as a monstrous interference with civil liberty, for which no adequate reason had been shown.—The Chairman said Mr. Meadowcroft had got a wrong expression. The Board never contemplated interference with competent schools such as had bees mentioned by Mr. Aleadowcroft. but with inefficient schools and inefficient teachers who evaded and did not promote the education of the town. (Applause.)— Dr. McDougall agreed with this statement, and said the resolution of the Board simply author- iced the Clerk to ascertain what powers the Board had in the matter.—Mr. Humphreys admitted Mr. Pritchard's claim, and said having regard to the estension of the work of the Board there ought to be an increase in the number of members of the Board. In order to save a contest at that season, he would with- draw could an arrangement be made for continuing the present Board in office, with a provision made for some- one to be put in Mr. Dalkeld's place.—Mr. Frith pro- posed that the present Board continue in office with Mr. Imison in place of Mr. Salkeld.—Mr. Hankinson thought they could not do better, and he withdrew his candida- ture. Alter anotherpause Mr. T. J. Norman said there ssemed to he a lot of heating about the bush. The Da- dependents were quite satisfied to let the Board remain in its present condition.—Mr. Meadowcroft was not yet eatisfied about the private schools, and Mr. Moss said there had been one school which was only a refuge for bad attenders, and this had now been closed. There was no complaint generally against the private schools. Mradowcroft said that was a considerable relief. .Another pause caused Mr. Humphreys to say it was to be hoped that the candidates would use more despatch than they were doing that night when they got on the Board.. The position of the Independent was clear, and they ought to be informed what was the position of the Church candidates.—Another long pause, then Mr. Taylor said he failed to see what they were sitting there for. The Independents had expressed their views as to the lines on which a contest could be avoided ; and they had waited a long time for a response. from the Church candidates hut none was forthcoming. Therefore the best plan would be to let the ratepayers decide the point. (Hear, hear.) He should go in for an election. After the expression the Church candidates and some of the nominators retired into the room, and upon returning, about ten minutes later, the vicar an- nounced tbat Mr. Cropper's resignation would be sent in.—Mr. Meadoacroft said he had been requested to announce the result of the consultation. Mr. 'misses still remained a candidate. Mr. Timmins also stated he would remain a candidate, he would not withdraw. Mr. Imison had expressed modified ideas on the questions of private schools, Mr. Timmins had not expressed any views whatever ; Dr. McDougall had satisfied him en- tirely. He (Mr. Meadowcroft) withdrew as an inde- pendent candidate, although not invited to Mr. Taylor's ineeting—(laughter)—and he should support - Dr. McDougall as an independent candidate.—Mr. Frith proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman.—Mr. Brun-e drit seconded. He presumed the end of it was ther_ would be a contest.—The Chairman : Yes.—Mr. Brun. drit : Right.—The meeting then concluded—The inde pendent candidates and their nominators,,, retired to the Beard room upstairs to consider their position. They were accompanied by Dr. McDougall and. Mr. Brundrit. When they had been discussing the situation some time. the Vicar, who had bean in consulta- tion with Mr. Imson, Mr. Timmins, and Mr. Joseph Pritchard sent in a proposition to the effect that they would accept Dr. McDougall on the under- standing that he considered lihnselfsa Church nominee. This was acceptsd, but Dr. McDougall. reserved to him- self perfect liberty of action on the Board. It was, therefore, annoianced that the nesessary witlideawals would be made-, and a contest avoided. The constitution of the Board will practically remain unchanged, only Mr. Imison taking the place of Mr. A. Salkeld.

div.head: HOMESTEAD POISONING PL,W.,'
div.p: THE HOMESTEAD POISONING PL,W.,'

21.—Patrick Gallagher, the cook who revealed the alleged plot; to poison the non-uxionist hands at the Carnegie Mills,. was arrested to-day and takeri to prison. Davidson, the cook's assistaat,. sur- rendezted to the warrant :aimed for his arrest, arid was released on bail. It is reported to-day :that three more noruoionist workpeople have died at Homestead under suspicious circmnstances, and it. is believed that they-also have been poisoned. The district coroner has accordingly deeided that the bodlts of all workers at the mills who have recently died under circumstances where there ;might be any doubt as to the cause of citath shall be eshilmed and sub:booted to a post-mortem examination. The matter is wow, being considered by the tirand Jury. Mr.Christitk an official of the Carnegie Company, to-day made the following statement I knovy that 32 men have dird of piston, but this is not all. Many others, some of whom will appear at the trial, are dying on their feet. Since wo began this tatruiry we have been startled by the. number of letters we have received from every part c. 2 the country from non-unionists who sickened of the prevailing complaint at Homestead, and went to their homes. Some ot these are still ill, and all are confident that they were poisoned. Altogether we had 4,000 men, employed during the strike of whom 2,000 siekene4, mau being toi v.eits cf 3 the wrge ot the greve;.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS.
DISTRIBITTION Or PRIZES BY MRS. BRUNNER.

Runcorn Public Hall was crowded on Monday evening, on the occasion of the annual distribution of prizes to the children attending Greenway-road Board Schools,who had been distinguished by punc- tual and regular attendance, and by successful school-work. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood,vice- chairman of the School Board, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. P. Wiswall, J. Pritchard, S.Taylor. J. R. frith, W. Hankinson, T. Handley, G.Moss, and J. D. Jones. The ceremony of presenting the prizes was gracefully performed by Mrs. Brunner. Mr. Brunner, M.P., had been announced to deliver an address,but, as the Chairman explained, he had con- tracted a severe cold, and he had not deemed it prudent to leave the south of france,and return to this inc.' :ment climate. The proceedings commenced by a choir of boys and girls singing the Christmas carol "God rest you. merry gentlemen," and then the Standard IV. girls recited the " Wreck f the Hesperus," which- was illus- trated with limelight views,hv a lantern manipulated by' Mr. E. R. Lea and Mr. C. Handley. Nursery rhymes by the younger children, dressed in character, was an enjoyable performance ; and after the part song, " Forest echoes," had been rendered, a dialogue entitled rue Trial of Ignorance" was given, the cast being as follows t—Sam Duace (the Prisoner), James Taylor; Baron Legality (the Judge), Rickard Shaw ; Mr. Puzzle (Counsel for the Prosecution), Joseph Savage ; Mr. Grip (Counsel for the Defence), John Catterall ;Twelve Jury- men ; Foreman of Jury, Bettie Eden ; Mr. Snap (School- master, witness), James A. Hill ; Mr. Pen (Schoolmaster. witness), Val. Drayson), Me. Press (Printer, wit- ness), Samuel Barker ; Mr. Fig (Grocer, witness), James Banner ; John Dunce (Prisoner's Father, witness), Alfred Goodier ; Police Constable, B. Cooper. The characters were very creditably pourtrayed. This concluded the first pirt of the programme. In the second part several part songs and carols were given, and there was a highly successful table, " Mrs. Jarley'a Waxworks," which after the operatien of " winding up,"went through some amusing movement.s. The performance of the " Ten nigger boys " was highly mirth-provoking and an encore was awarded. The song" Cockles alive" by Edith McLean, Edith Wright, and Blanche Baxley, was appreciated. The entire en- tertainment was highly pleasing, and credit is due to the head teachers and their assistants, for the time and trouble they must have spent in training the young people so successfully in the several parts. During the interval in tho programme, the Chairman ascended the platform, accompanied by Mrs. Brunner, who was presented with a beautiful bouquet by Miss Edith McLean. In the course of a speech, the Chairman described the system upon which the prizes had been awarded, and impressed upon those present the importance of punctuality both for the benefit ot the children and of the school. It was only fair that they should be told that no use whatever was made of the rates, in order to provide the prizes. He said this advisedly, because it had been as- serted that it wae comparatively easy for the Board School to provide the prises, seeing that they could be paid for out of the rates. In justice and fairness they ought to understand that not one single farthing had been derived, or would be derived, from the rates, for such a purpose. (Applause.) Then it might be asked " How are the prizes paid for?" It was hy the enter- prise and energy of the teachers of the school. (Ap- plause.) They had been during the past year giving entertainments, some of which had returned consider- able profit, and especially that at which Mr. Lynners- ley, her Majesty's Inspector of Schools, gave a lecture. The money thus made had been devoted to defray the expenses of those prews. The schoolmaster, Mr. Moul- ton, had had the wisdom to provide himself, little by little, with the assistance of others, with a very nice magic lantern. He thought he should like to add, as Mrs. Brunner was present, that it was not very ldng since Mr. Brunner offered to give the Board a magic lantern, but they answered that it was unnecessary, as they already possessed, one. The hon. gentleman was then kind enough to send about £lO worth of slides for the lantern. (Applause.) Mrs. Branner then proceeded with the distribution, the recipients numbering about 200. Mr. Pritchard said they had witnessed with a degree of pleasure the ceremony of presenting the priws, so patiently performed by Mrs. Brunner. They all felt deeply grateful to her for honouring them with her presence, and for showing her sympathy with the work being accomplished in their Board School. He asked them to accord her a hearty vote of thanks for her services. _ _

Mr. Wiswall seconded the proposition. They all knew the great interest Mr. and Mrs. Brunner took in the matter of education, They were also aware what a grand thing education was. It was far cheaper than ignorance. He saw a striking insti.nce of that fact the other day, when Mr. West, the Recorder of Manchester, stated that since the introduction of the Education Act crime in Manchester had been reduced by two-thirds. Tha-. was one proof of the value of education. They regretted very muan that Mr. Brunner was unable to be present, but they hoped he would soon be better, and able to continue his work of forwarding the import- ant cause of education. (Applause.) The motion was carried with prolonged cheering. Mrs. Brunner. in acknowledging the compliment. thanked the audience very much for their kind welcome. She was very pleased to have had the opportunity of distributing the prizesto the children and of witnessing their performance. She was sorry her husband was not able to be present, but she had cometo do her best in his absence. (Applause.) Mr. J. R. Frith proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman. He congratulated the members of the School Board upon the great success of the schools, and ex- pressed the hope that the good work would continue to prosper.—Mr. T. Handley seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT OF TIMBER AT LONGFORD.

At the borough police court, on Saturday, Thomas O'Day, John Smith and Darby Fahey were charged with stealing from Longford gas works the previous evening a quantity of timber, value is., the property of John Taylor, a contractor, residing at Garston, and now carry- ing on a contract for the Corporation at the gas works. —P.C. Delahaye and another constable deposed to meet- ng the men coming from the works carrying the wood.— The defence of O'Day and Fahey was that they were carrying it home for firewood, and they did not think there was any harm in this. Smith said he was simply carrying wood for O'Day, and O'Day said that was true. —The Chief Constable said he did not wish to press the case. Mr. Taylor merely wished to stop this practice of carrying away wood.—Smith was dismissed, and the other prisoners were fined 23. 6d. each. THE CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. The adjourned case of Thomas Mitchell, and Celia his wife, of Latchford, who had been twice remanded on a charge of wilful neglect of their children, was called. Mr. J. D. Buckton, the prosecuting solicitor, said after the first remand there had .been very little improvement

in the condition of the children, but now there was a great deal, and they seemed to be properly treated. He would, therefore, with the permission of the Bench, withdraw the case. The application was acceded to.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

Savartai.::Before Mr. J. Burgess (chairman) Alderman Chandley and Mr. S. Wright. Trtarr or Boom.—William Parry was charged with stealing en the previous evening, from the shop door of Mersrs. Boothman and Co., LA., 2, Buttermarket-street, a pair of boots, value 7s. 6d.—William Brown, manager for the firm, who was not sworn, identified the boots, produced.—Robert Lowe, estate agent, whose office is next door to the prosecutors' shop, said the prisoner and two other men were standing with their backs to his door. One of the men with the prisoner tried to lift the boots off the shop door, and another man, not the prisoner, lent him a knife with which he cut the string. He threw the boots on to the office steps. Witness immedi- ately informed the wife of the shop manager, and she came out and got the boots, with which the prisoner did not get away. He also informed a constable who took the man in charge.—The Chairman commended Mr. Lowe for his services, but informed the shop manager that he ought not to hang his goods out, as it was expos- ing men to temptation and it was therefore an improper practice, but for which the prisoner would not have been in court.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. NON-MAINTENANCE OF A IFE . —James Lee was charged, on a warrant, with non-payment of arrears, 425., for the . maintenance of his wife, a tobacconist.—lt was remarked that she only brought the proceedings to prevent him annoying her at the shop.—The defendant said he only went to buy tobacco.—lle was sent to jail for a month.
MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Alderman Greenall (chairman), Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. J. W. Hayward. •

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —Patrick Moor, in Church- st., on Saturday night, ss.—Wm. Brown. in Mersey-st., en Sunday morning, ss. and costs. —Annie Smith, in Buttexmarket-at., on Sunday morning, s.—Mary Ann Kenyon, in Knutsford-road, on Sunday night, 53. ASSAULT—John Jordan, labourer, was charged with assaulting John Williams,at Bank Quay Railway Station, on Saturday night. The complainant said the defen- dant had, without provocation, pushed him down and kicked him in the third class waiting room, and he called witnesses to prove this.—The defendant said the com- plainant had provoked him by insulting him. ss. and costs. JUVEI•ZILIS GAMBLERS.—James Dickinson, John-st., Wm. Coyne, Scotland-road, John Griffin, Scotland-road, and Edward Dooney, 7, Buckley's Court, all boys, were charged with playing at cards for money, off Foundry- St., on Sunday morning.—Dickinson and Dooney were fined Zs. 6d., and the others ss. each.—Some money taken from the lads, was, as usual, in such cases, put into the poor box. KNOCICTON Aomx.—Wm. Farrell, Cropper's Brow, Bodelia Knockton, and Annie Johnson, 3, Naylor-st., were charged that they being persons of notorious character, were found frequenting Butterrnarket-st., on Saturday afternoon, with intent to commit a felony.— D.S. Monaghan deposed that he found Farrell wearing a pair of boots, a waistcoat and a pair of socks, which he had not on the previous day, and the female pri- soners were each wearing a new skirt and a new shawl. He followed them into a public-house, and took them to the police station, and asked them to account for the new things they had on. Johnson said she and Knock- ton were with a fellow the night before and Knock- ton took a purse containing 333. from him and bought the things with the money. The male prisoner said he bought his new things, but Johnson said "No, you Bodelia bought and paid for them." Farrell be- haved disgracefully at the police station. He cohabited with Knockton, and had just done six months' imprison- ment with hard labour.—After other evidence, the pri- soners were each sentenced to three months' imprison- ment with hard labour.—Knockton : This is not a fair trial. You are no men. _ . - - - .
AN OBJECTIONABLE FEMALE.—Bridget Lally for using unseemly language in Buttermarket-street, on the 6th inst., ss. and costs._

AN INSANITARY LODGING HODSE.—William Cobley, common lodging-house keeper, Old-road, was charged by Ralph Nornaan, inspector of nuisances, under six counts, with various offences, on the 14th, inst.,against the sanitary laws, which consisted of neglect to keep clean his lodging house and out premises, and omitting to provide a sufficient number of basins and towels.—Mr. P. Davies defended.—Mr. Norman deposed to the cir- cumstances. Cobley, he said, had also a lodging-house at Runcorn, and lived there, leaving the house at Latch- ford in charge of a deputy.—Mr. Norman said he was in- structed to apply that the license of this house should be withdrawn, until the necessary alterations were made.— In reply to Mr. Davies, Mr. Norman admitted that from what he knew the defendant was a respectable man, and that the lodging-house was kept in a very different con- dition when he lived there himself.—Mr. Davies said Mr. Garnett, Alderman Wright, and Mr. Hunt had visited the house, and then expressed their satisfaction with it. The defendant would undertake to discharge his deputy, or do anything that was required on condition that he was not convicted. Those who used the house were nearly al! navvies, and as many of this class had left the district there would not be the same accommodation re- quired. It had accommodation for 100 people, and there had not been a case of sickness in it during the last 4 years.—The Chief-Cot st ible gave the defendant an ex- cellent character.—The defendant was convicted on each of the six courts, and fined ss. and costs for each offence, his license not being withdrawn. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Daniel Roberts, bus' driver, 28, Powys-street, was charged with working a horse on the 15th inst.,while it was in an unfit state, and Thomas Wright, horse-keeper, of Rylands-street, with causing it to be worked.—P.C. Jones, another constable, and Inspector Dow ty, R.S.P.C.A., deposed to the animal suffering from a wound which rendered it unfit to be at work.—Mr. Dowty exonerated Roberts from blame as being compelled to obey instructions.—The horse- keeper's defence was that the horse was all right when cot out.—The Bench dismissed the eases, it being

remarked that they knew Roberts to be the oldest driver in town, and a very careful man. FIGHTING WOMEN.—LIKE DOGS OR CATS P—Elizabeth Ellen Fleming and Ellen Davies, of 3, Naylor-street, were charged with fighting in that street on the 14th inst.---P.C. Baxendale said they werefighting like dogs.—The Magis- trates' Clerk Were they biting one another ?—Witness: Mrs. Fleming had her hands in the other's hair. —The Magistrates' Clerk : That was more like oats. (Laughter.) The defendants were each bound over to keep tke peace. CHIMNEYS ON FlRB.—Margaret Tomlinson, Henry Critchley, George Dunbobbin, and Bridget Leonard, were fined is. each, for having their chimneys on I fire.

TuEsnAr.—Beforo Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair), E. J. Guest, and Dr. Starkey Smith. YOUTHFUL GAMBLERS.—James Walton, Peter Kelly, and John Moores, three boys,were charged with playing at "pitch and toss," in Palmyra-square, on Monday. P,C. Hampson proved the charge, and the boys were detained in the police station for the day and a convic- tion was recorded against them. INspxcroic 111Lxv's Struixers.—The following persons were dealt with at the evidence of Inspector Riley, school attendance officer :—Elizabeth Moores, William- st., Ambrose Foden, Halifax-st.,Richard Booth, Warbur- ton-st., Frank Leigh, Brierly-st., James Mosley, Beswick-st. DRUNKENNESS.—Maggie Leonard, of no fixed abode, and Michael Allen, a Ship Canal navvy, were both sent to jail for seven days for drunkenness.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. G. Geddes.
HE DIDN'T INTEND TO GIVE HIMSELF up.—Samuel Hill, a navvy, was sent to jail for seven days for going to the police station in a drunken condition the previous even- ing. • - • -

FRlDAY.—Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), Councillor J. H. Fleming, and Mr. S. Wright. SAID "Sao WOULD SWING FOR HER."—Maly Dono- hue, Friar's Green, was charged with using threats to Mary Melia, married woman, of Dolman's-lane.—The evidence showed that some time ago the prosecutrix appeared as a witness against the defendant,on a charge of neglecting her children. Since then the complainant said she had constantly threatened her, and on Saturday last said" she would swing for her."—Bound over to keep the peace for six months. HAD TO PAY FOR His FUN.—Patrick Higgins, an Irish farm labourer, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly at Bank Quay Station, the previous night, and further with impeding one of the company's officers in the execution of his duties. The case was proved by Detective Win. Osborne, in the employ of the Railway Company.—Fined ss. and costs for drunkenness, and 10s. and costs for the other offence.

• in with a minor. For some time the Old Boys had a lot the best of the argument, their forwards and backs playing splendidly, and a further exhibition of weakness by the home backs let in Cooper, who scored by the posts, the try being converted. On another occasion Bryon fielded the ball beautifully, and ran round his men, but the visiting touch judge ruled his man in touch ' to the evident disgust of the would-be try-getter. With darkness rapidly approaching, and the homesters only 14 men, Smith having had to retire after the first half, it looked odds on the visitors, for despite the injunctions of the somewhat disappointed onlookers, the Warring- ton team continued to play in the same disjointed fashion. Then Lally made a couple of splendid runs, but the score was unaltered until the last few minutes, when Jolley seizing possession made a superb effort, and succeeded in getting a brilliant try. On Barnes de- pended the anal touch, but he was equal to the occasion, and kicked an unmistakable goal, the match ending in a draw. WARRINGTON STAR V. COCRIIRDG3 ROVERS. —This match was played at Longford, and after a rough game ended in a win for the Star by 1-1-8 to 1 minor. Corcoran and Costello scored the tries, and H. Knight kicked the goal. The Star backs played a grand dashing game. Jeffers, Hanamersley and Makinson were the pick of the forwards.

STOCKTON HEATH V. FARNWORTH.—PIayed at Farn- worth. The visitors kicked off, and after several ex- changes play settled in midfield. From some loose play the homesters took the ball over the visitors' line, but only a minor resul.:ed. The drop-out found the Heathen- ites pressing, the homesters having to touch down twice in succession. After this neither side could make much progress, until shortly before half-time, when Broady obtained a pass intended for his opponent, raced up the field, and gained a try, Baldwin failing at the place. The second half commenced in darkness. Some neat passing between Gregory, Cross, and Broady almost had effect. From some off-side play the homesters took the ball up the field, and at this point of the game, on ac- count of the referee's decisions, the visitors found it advisable to leave the field in darkness, the score then being—Stockton Heath, 1 try, 4 minors ; Farnworth, 1 minor. RUNCORN RECREATION V. DALLAM BRHWERY.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday. The Dallam team arrived early, but the Recreation were same time in getting a team together. In the end they turned out with 14 men, being short of Clarke and Nickson, who was playing with Runcorn "A "team, and Abel Roden, Johnson, Jones, and Whitney, for whom substitutes had to be found. However, the team that represented the Recs. played together splendidly. The Brewery men kicked off uphill, and a good return being made, play settled in the visitors' quarter, where it remained the greater portion of the first half. Molyneaux made his mark in a favourable position, and Gregory easily landed:a goal. The Recreation men kept up the attack, and after Carruthers had just missed scoring,Mclyneaux got over from a line out. Carr kicked a goal, but the referee only allowed the try. Half time arrived with the score Recreation one goal, one try, and five minors, to nil. In the second half play was not so good, the Brewery men playing with the incline and being a much heavier team having a great advantage, but the Recs. played up hard, and nothing further was scored. The match ended in a win for the Recreation, by one goal, one try, and six minors to Dallam Brewery nil.

div.head: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
Wamiasnair.-IBefore Major Pickmere (in the chair) and
Mr. -Mortimer.

PICKING Cash.—Mary Topping, of Burtonwood, was charged with stealing, on the 21st November, a ton of coal from the premises of the Collins Green Colliery Company. The evidence showed that the defendant, like many other persons in the neighbourhood, had been in the habit of picking scrap coal from a refuse heap, on the Company's premises. Fined is. and cost. DHUNKENNESS.—John Hughes, fined ss. for being drunk at Sankey Bridges on Sunday night.—Thomas Rouskin, jun. of Croft, 2s. 6d. and costs. SHOOTING 1:TA.3113 noisoN.—Jonas Collins Winwick- at., was summoned for shooting, on Saturday last, a tame pigeon, value 10s., the property of Joseph Parr.— Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the prosecution, said it was a common thing for men to wantonly shoot tame pigeons, generally prize birds, which pigeon fanciers " flew" in that neighbourhood. If they found the de- fendant guilty he hoped they would punish him in an exemplary manner for the benefit of the persons keep- ing those prize birds. The facts of the case were that on Saturday prosecutor sent his brother Alfred to "throw up "the pigeon near the policeman's house in Winwick. Directly Alfred had" thrown up" the bird he heard a gun shot and saw the defendant in a field with a gun. He had shot the bird. He pursued the defendant. He went to a house in Catherine-st., and left his gun there, although he lived in Winwick-road. Defendant deniesl having shot the bird.—Alf red Parr, identified the defendant as the man who shot the bird. —Mr. John Fisher, farmer, Winwick, saw the pigeon shot, and saw the defendant run away.—Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for the defence, denied that his client knew anything about the pigeon being shot.— Defendant had to pay the cost of the pigeon and the costs. _ _ _ . _ _

A DESERTHR.—Wm. Fox, a deserter from the 3rd Battalion, West Riding Regiment, was ordered to await an escort. "WITHOUT A STAIN ON HIS Casu.scrsa."—Matthew Isherwood, who at one time carried on the business of a fustian cutter,at Warrington, was charged with stealing workmen's tools from a building in course of erection at Sankey Bridges. The articles,which included two trowels and a hammer,were the propierty of Thomas Taylor and Henry Easom, both of whom were engaged at the build- ing. Mr. Percy Davies defended. Evidence was given to the effect that two of the tools were sold by defendant at a second hand shop in Mersey-st. He afterwards went to the Police Station and made a statement that the articles had been given him to sell by another man. He was thereupon locked up,and handed over to the county police. Mr. Davies, in his address for the defence, said, although the police had received information from a boy who had tried to sell the tools, which were afterwards sold by defendant, that the man from whom he received them was about 30 years of age, and had plaster on his trousers, they locked defendant up. He said he should not be doing his duty as a solicitor if he did not report the matter, and he asked for prisoner to be discharged without a "a stain on his character."—The Beach, after hearing the evidence for the defence, decided to dismiss the case.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies.

GONE Home TO HIS MOTHER.—George Dutton was charged under a warrant with neglecting to maintain his wife and family, at Runcorn.—Complainant stated that her husband left her three weeks ago that morning. She was in lodgings. She had two children, add this was the sixth or seventh time he had gone from her within a year and five months. He belonged to Will- ington, Tarporley. and had gone home to his mother. He was a carter, and was able to earn 255. per week.-- Defendant alleged that he was out of work.—He was ordered to contribute 10s. per week towards the sup- port of his wife and children, and to pay the costs, 10s. 61

_ THEFT OF COAL.—Thomas Hulse. aged twelve years; William Ellis, eleven years ; and Henry Ellis, 14 years, were charged with stealing Scwts. of coal from a coal yard in Canal-st. on the previous night, the property of Henry Aldred.—The prisoners Hulse and William Ellis acknowledged the offence. but denied that Henry Ellis had anything to do with the theft.—Thomas Hulse and William Ellis were sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod, to be administered by P.C. Gregory, and Henry Ellis was discharged. SWEETS AND Birraas.—William Looker, Church-street, Runcorn, labourer, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Martha Looker.—Complainant stated that for some time she had been endeavouring to earn her living by boiling sweets. On the 13th inst„ she had been pre- paring some toffy, when her husband came in, hit her on the head, took hold ef her throat, and tried t break her arm.—Defendant said he was exasperated at a quantity of sugar having been spoilt. Mrs. Looker said she went about in fear of her life.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £5 and a surety of £lO, and ordered to pay the costs ; in default 14 days' imprisonment.—Defendant : I will have 14 days.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brock and G. Pilkington. DRUNKENNRIS.—James Dixon, Cadishead ; John Creahon, no fixed abode ; Patrick Riley, Pitt-street ; Thomas McCann, Warrington; William Griffiths, Sutton's-lane; Arthur Reid ; John and Annie Gaudy; and Mary Finnety, of no fixed abode, were each fined for this offence.

ASSAULTING THE Poucs.—George Mannion, of no fixed residence, was charged with having been drunic ad assaulting P.C. Jennings.—On Sunday afternoon prisoner was drunk in Victoria-street, and on being taken into custody became very violent, and kicked the constable seweral times on the leg.—Pris oner was ordered to pay 2s. Eid. and costs in each case, or 14 days in default.
SLEEPING 013 T.—Thomas Firth urst and Thomas Hagan no fixed abode, were charged with sleeping in a shed at Bold Colliery, and were sent to gaol for seven days.
MR. GLADSTONE'S DEPARTURE FOR
THE CONTINENT.

Amid a good deal of demonstration, the Premier, with Mrs. and Miss Gladstone and party left Folkestone at a quarter-past twelve on Wednesday, for Boulogne. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone spent the morning at the Pavilion Hotel, and at his special request Mr. Gladstone received a deputation of local political admirers was reluctantly declined. The quays in front of the Custom-house and the approaches to the harbour station were crowded- and as Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone passed on to the steamer repeated cheers were given. Both looked extremely well and in grand spirits. Just before the time of start log the fog lifted and the sun broke through. The sea was quite calm.
