div.p: RUGBY.

RUNCORN V. BROUGHTON Reea:ans.—At Broughton in the presence of 1,500 spectators, at 3.10 Jackson sent the ball in motion on behalf of the home side, and Kingston having his kick charged down. Hostilities at once raged in the home half, Chapman making his mark. The centre, however, was soon the scene of play, and Abram putting a fine dribble he ended by giving Robinson a good pass, the latter scoring a try, which Crompton converted. After the drop out mid- field was the venue of play for same time until the visit- ors gradually took operations in the home half. Wylde and Jackson neutralised this, however, with some good play, and Runcorn territory was invaded. It did not remain there long, as the visitors were playing a good game. Crompton next took a shot at the goal, a minor resulting. Upon resuming Kingston soon scored another try, after t having obtained possession from Crompton, the latter failing at goal. This seemed to arouse the Rangers, and in quick time Shaw scored a try, but he failed to improve from an easy position. Play was of a severe natiire,the Cestrians having, if anything, a little the best of it, and half-time came With the score—Run- corn, 1 goal, 1 try. Final result.—Runcorn 1 goal, 1 try; Broughton Rangers, 1 try. WIDNES V. BARTON.—Payed at Widnes, on Saturday. Both clubs were well represented. Barber started at 315 for Widnes, and play ruled even for some time. Wright and Hughes relieved some pressure on the part of the visitcrs, but they subsequently got away, and Brennan narrowly escaped letting them in. Widnes now forced the game, and several rushes were made for the Barton line, and eventually Drummond gave a splendid pass to Wright, who scored, but Brennan failed at goal. From the kick off Drummond returned to the visitors' quarter, and Drummond again started a pass, but Alford with a clear run before knocked on in trying to get possession. Alford, however, got away a few minutes later, and passed to Clarke, who scored near the corner flag but the point was not allowed. Half- time score— Widnes, 2 tries ; Barton' nil, which had not been altered when the whistle blew for "no side." RUNCORN HORNETS V. RUNCORN RANI:MRS.—This match was played at Bate's Bridge on Saturday in fine weather. The following represented the Rangers :—Full back, C. H. Cook ; threequarters, Hughes, J. Butterworth (cap- tain), A. Houghton ; half backs, E. Woodward, J. W. Johnson : forwards, T. Woods, W. Russell, W. Sutton, W. E. Hough, J. Brennan, S. Rowlinsen, J. Helsby, W. Faulkner, R. Miles: The Hornets losing the toss they kicked off down hill at 3.15, Hughes making a feeble return to touch the play settled in the Rangers" 25." Gradually the play was worked te half way, Gayter essayed a run but was tackled by Hughes. Numerous scrimmages now took place. Percival got hold and passed to Worthington and he to Gayter who took off along touch until Woodward put a stop to his career. The Gornets by hard forward play pressed the Rangers I to their line where the play remained of a scrambling I nature for a few minutes until Johnson and Woodward relieved by a short run. Two minors now fell to the Hornets from strong kicks by Jolley. Half-time score. Hornets, 2 minors; Rangers, nil. On resuming, the Rangers pressed hard and were within an ace of scoring from forward dribbling, the ball unfortunately striking in the mud. The remainder of the game was of a wretched character, being a mare forward scramble, the Rangers backs scarcely ever handling the ball, Final result, Hornets, 3 minors ; Rangers, nil. Referee, Mr. J. L eathwood.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

The visit to Cavendish Park, Barrow, is one of the most enjoyable outings' on the Warrington card, and there was no wonder to find on Saturday almost a full complement of players turning up to do duty. Jolley was the only absentee from the original team selected, the vacancy letting in Hampson. Matches have beenin progress with Barrow for eight years, and during that time only two victories have been secured by the Furness men, once on their native heath, whilst last season they accounted for a weak team of our local men. On arriving at Barrow a slow drizzling rain pre veiled, and this following a heavy fall nearly the whole of Friday, it will be readily gathered that the game was fought under considerable disadvantage. Barrow was fully representative, and about 1,500 per- sons lined the ropes when Turner kicked off. Jones' reply was met by-Webster, and at the onset Warrington was in an aggressive mood. From a scrimmage at the Barrow quarter flag a smart pass from Bate was as equally well taken by Evans, who dodged in splendid style, and when his opponents had been drawn to hire he coolly placed the oval in the hands of Lawless, the latter putting the finishing touch on as fine a bit of com- bination as one need see. The place was too difficult for Turner to utilise. By judicious kicking Heesom and Webster prevented the Barrow forwards from clearing their quarter flag, and a dribble by Ashton, Berry, and Hampson afforded Baker an excellent opportunity of ' displaying his saving powers. Jones, however, got in a free kick, only to have it negatived by Bate and Evans, who both kicked in turn, eventually reaching Kelly, this smart Birkenhead Wanderers player making his mark. Boscow met the charge with safety, and his kick being seconded by some ' brilliant work by Nevins and Heesom, Barrow fell back on their lines. The Furness forwards stuck manfully to their work, but Webster dribbled t. the line, and Berry got over, but a minor point was all that was allowed. Whrrington next lost ground by over- eagerness, and the free kick to Barrow saw the homes- tars pegging away at the visitors' lines. The defence was stubborn, and eventually Webster, Teare, Nevins, and Turner all aided in the relief, which realized the half-way flag. A grand run by Kelly once more placed the game on the Warrington line, and only fine tackling prevented the Cheshire County man from getting in. Turner and Ashton ably led the Warringtonians to more desirable quarters, and fine play by Lawless saw Baker getting well under weight and Warrington once more on the defensive. Boscow was hard pressed, but proved equal to the emergency, but Jones taking up a dribble from near half-way, a misunderstanding between Webs- ter and Boscow saw Guirdwood rushing up and placing the sides on equal terms, the same player failing at the difficult place. A feeble reply to Turner's drep-out by Dickenson saw Bate dropping nicely to the Borrow quar- ter flag, and Turner, from a line-out, rushed down with excellent dash, Baker just saving. Thrice Warrington were within an ace of scoring, but from an erratic pass to Heesom Dickenson intercepted, and promptly placed the oval at half-way. Berry dribbled accurately, but received little assistance in his last effort, but another display of overeagerness spoiled a grand opening. A penalty kick fell to Warrington a minute later, and Webster taking the kick had the ill-luck to hit the posts, I and Marshall and Chapman ran the oval out. Another minor fell to Warrington from another rush, and half- tme arrived with the score as Warrington, 0-1-2 ; Bar- w, 0-1-0. On resuming, the play opened in a vigorous manner, and early on Barrow showed signs of attack. They were repulsed by Heesom, Boscow, and Turner, and only for the fine play of Kelly Barrow's goal must assuredly have fallen. Some pretty passing by the Barrow backs saw Kelly being collared near the Warrington lines, and Moore eventually dribbled past Boscow, but luckily danger was averted by a save on the part of a Warring- tonian. Berry now showed up with a fine dribble to the Barrow quarters, but Kelly was the saviour of his side, running the oval back to the half-way flag. An excel- lent piece of play between Evans, Bate, and Lawless led up to the latter placing Warrington on the attack, and from some exchange kicking two of the visitors collided —Randle. and Hampson—the former having to retire with his nose broken. Hampson was damaged about the head, and was practically no use after, though he fell back to the three-quarter ranks for the remainder of the game. Baker saved finely on several occasions, and despite the fact that Warrington were minus the services of two good forwards, the seven got down to their work and held the opposing nine in check. Berry again demonstrated his capabilities in the dribbling art, but a call for a pass saw his confreres knocking on, and a grand chance was lost. From cross dribbling by Evans and 11 Bate, Lawless was held on the line' and Turner looked al scorer from a pass by Bate, until Moore floored him. Boscow was now called upon from an effort by Marshall and Chapmon, and the rush which ensued saw Nevins getting in, but again the verdict was against the visitors the third minor being sent up. Vigorous forward play was the remaining feature of the matah, and as this was almost confined to neutral quarters, the game did mot call for much comment. Final score :—Warrington, 0-1-3; Barrow, 0-1-0. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back ; H. Webster, F. Heesom, and P. R. Lawless, three-quarters ; John Bate and John Evans, half backs ; 11. Ashton (captain), Fair. Turner, W. Nevins, J. Berry, W. Bandies, J. T. Thormley, H. Teare, J. Holmes, and G. Hampson, forwards. Barrow: Baker, back ; Kelly, T. Dickinson, and Harley, three-quarters ; Marshall and Chapraan, half backs ; Weatherall, Parker, Satterthwaite, Girdwood, J. Jones, E. Dickinson, Smith, Bowker, and Moore, forwards. Mr. S. Pollitt, of Swinton, officiated as referee. WARRINGTON A v. FAILSWORTIC OLD Bars—There were not so many spectators as one would have anticipated for this encounter, although the mildness of the weather was inviting enough, but no doubt the lateness of the arrival of the visitors caused a considerable number to wend their steps Howley way, where,:under the auspices of the Junior Competition, a contest of keen rivalry was being fought. As regards the match under notice little description is requisite, as for more than half the 50 minutes agreed to be played it was almost impossible to individualize the combatants across the ground. Fails- worth commenced with some capital footwork, and, aided by the sureness of their backs, soon had their opponents defending, who were lucky enough in escap-

div.head: WARRINGTON JUNIOR LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON JUNIOR LEAGUE.

PARISH CHURCH V. RANGERS.—This important match in the above competition was played on Saturday, when a large crowd assembled on the Parish ground to witness the struggle. Both teams turned out as advertised, and in the opening stages the visitors held the upper hand. After a smart piece of play by Deakin, Clare scored near the posts, no goal resulting. This early reverse roused the Churehites, and encouraged by their supporters, the game was transferred to the other end. Carey was almost over after some pretty play, and Welsby also had hard lines. Half-time arrived with the score unaltered, and the visitors crossed over with a lead of two points. The second half after the opening exchanges settled down into a continued attack on the Rangers' strong- hold, and Welsby secured the first try. This was not improved on, and the teams were level. Carey was loudly applauded for a brilliant run, and as the result of some pretty play in the loose by the home forwards the same player succeeded in crossing the line. No advan- tage accrued from the place kick. but, playing with re- markable dash, the Churchites held their lead to the end, and were unfortunate in not increasing their score. Final result :—Parish Church,two tries (four points) ; Rangers, one try (two points). Referee, Mr. E. Gilbert.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON CBIC/EBY CLUB Y. BROOKLANDS.—The Cricket Club, after a months enforced idleness, met Brooklands. at Brooklands, on Saturday. The game was exceedingly fast. The Cricket Club kicked off, and at once took the ball down to the Brooklands end, and were very nearly scoring on two occasions. After the game was about ten minutes old the Brooklands forwards got away, and the centre opened the score. A few minutes later they again scored. The Cricket Club forwards, however, were doing most of the pressing and Barlow had hard lines in not scoring, a hard shot Cy him hitting the cross-bar, rebounding into play ; but a few seconds later Reid kicked the first gnat for the visitors. The game was very even until half-time, nothing further being scored. After restarting the Brooklands forwards pressed repeatedly, and their shooting was so good that four more goals were added to them, while the Cricket Club only managed to score once, Hoare kicking the second goal for them. A very pleasant game thus ended in favour of Brooklands by 6 goals to 2. Cricket Club team :—Goal, J. Forrest •, full backs, L. Smith and J. S. Francomb •, half backs, Kenyon F. Williamson, and W. D. Jeans ; forwards, Hannah,A. R. Hoare, E. Jones, J. C. Barlow, and W. Reid. FRI/ENDS' SCHOOL, PENIEETTI,7I7, FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL,—This match was played on Saturday, at Farn- worth. Penketh pressed at the outset, and Limney scored. The right wing then had a turn, and Reynolds by a good shot made the score equal. Farnworth then had a look in, and Harrison scored their only goal. For Penketh, Limney after some capital work on the wing, again scored, and the same player put another through from a splendid pass from the right. After half-time, playing against the wind, Penketh scored thrice— Smith two and Reynolds one. Penketh finally won by seven goals to one. Lewis at back was in grand form, and so was Wilkinson at centre half, whilst the forwards played prettily on many occasions.

WARRINGTON ST. ELPHIN'S RESIRVE V. PADGATE.— This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. St. Eiphin's kicked off, and for a time play was in midfield, till the Saints rushed the ball down the field, Colley shooting wide. Padgate now played up, and from a scrimmage in goal Howard seared the first goal for Pad- gate. Just before half-time Bradshaw, with a good shot equalized. In the second half Smith scored for the Saints. Final result :—St. Elphin's Reserve, 2 ; Pad- gate, 1.

WARRINGTON RESTIRTE v. LYMM RESHRTB.—The above teams met at Arpley on Slturday, in fine weather, the ground being in a muddy state. Lyrnm kicked off against a slight breeze, and made backs for Hayes, but Ls.wton relieved. The homesters, settling down to work played a nice passing game, and from a combined run Thompson put in a strong shot, which was returned to be met by the same player scoring. Radford next scored from a neat run, and the left wing, gaining pos- session, raced away, and T. Mather passing back to E. Mather, the latter player scored a grand overhead goal. The home team still kept up the pressure, but half-time arrived with—Warrington three goals; Lymm, nil. Re- starting, the visitors went off with some dash, but were quickly repulsed by Parrott. The home forwards worked the sphere to the opposite end, Thompson scor- ing. Lymm now played up, and sticking well to their work went ahead towards Hayes, S. Bradburn scoring their only point. This livened the home team up con- siderably, as they had been playing very laggardly, and, settlingilown to their work, severely penned in their opponents, E. Mather scoring two more goals for War- rington, the whistle sounding for time with the score— Warrington, six goals ; Lymm, one.

div.head: NORTHAMPTON MURDER.
div.p: THE NORTHAMPTON MURDER.
TRIAL OF MACRAE.

The trial of Andrew George Macrae for the murder of Annie Pritchard was continued at Northampton Assizes, on Thursday. It is stated that towards the end of July the prisoner bought a quantity of lime and hired two conveyances. The apparel—believed to be Annie Prit- chard's—that he had sold to clothes dealers was identified by the purchasers. One witness said, he saw a dense mass of smoke coming ont of the warehouse chimney be- tween July 8 and 27. There was also a fearful smell. Mr. Justice Kennedy thought the jury would attach little im- portance to statements of that kind. The police evidence also aroused comment from his Lordship. The prisoner was taken to the police station at Northampton in order to tell his story about the clothing. He said it had been sent to him by his wife in a tin box. The police, after 'inquiry, detained him, and he was questioned by an inspector. Mr. Justice Kennedy said the duty of the police was not to interrogate a person charged to make him a witness against himself. Mr. Buszard, for the prosecution, said the prisoner was not actually in custody at the time. The Judge said he failed to understand the difference. Now he knew that the man was detained,he should certainly rule that the statements he made then were inadmissible. Lizzie Pritchard, the sister of the murdered woman, said she had heard of Guy Anderson, and understood that Annie left Birmingham to marry him.

div.head: DEATH OF SIR RICHARD OWEN.
div.p: DEATH OF SIR RICHARD OWEN.

Sir Richard Owen died on Sunday morning, at Sheen Cottage, Richmond Park. Sir Richard was born at Lancaster in 1804, and received his preliminary education in his native town. He was then articled to a surgeon, and in 1823 entered the University of Edinburgh. Dur- his residence in Edinburgh, he assisted in founding the HunterianiMedical Society, of' which he was president in 1825; and for more than forty years, until it ceased to be a students' debating club, took an active interest in its welfare. In 1826 he removed to London, and joined the Medical School of St. Bartholomew's Hospital, taking the diploma of the College of Surgeons in the same year. His first scientific paper was written during his stay here, having been read to the Medical Society of the Hospital School; and from 1830 paper after paper, work after work poured from his pen, each containing some remarkable discovery or unfolding some new view in comparative anatomy. In 1856 he was appointed Sup- erintendent of the Natural History Department of the British Museum. The various volumes of the printed catalogue, which constitute pathological and anatomi- cal works of the most elaborate character, were for the most part by him, though it was not until his "Memoir on the Pearly Nautilus" appeared that his merits attracted general attention. still continuing to enlarge and describe Hunter's Museum, he not only issued several other volumes descriptive of its riches, but in 1837 edited Hunter's "Animal Economy" and other papers ; twenty-four years later publishing two other volumes of Hunter's unpublished writings on anatomy and natural history, and prefacing both issues with elaborate dissertations on the contributions which their author made to the sum of knowledge. As early as 1834 he had begun to lecture on comparative anatomy at St. Bartholomew's, and in 1836 he became a professor of anatomy and physiology to the Royal College of Surgeons, and in the same year Hun- terian professor. In these capacities, as well as during His different tenures of the Fullerian Chair of Physiology in the Royal Institution, he delivered annual courses of I lectures which for many years were " institutions" in London, attracting not only ordinary ordinary students, but distinguished members of the medical profession and laymen of high rank. In 1883 he retired from the super- intendence of the Natural History Department of the British Museum, and was nominated a K.C.B.,the minor distinction of C.B. having been bestowed some years previously. Sir Richard Owen had in addition received almost every honour which comes within the grasp of men of science. In 1858 he presided over the Leeds meeting of the British Association, and for many years he had en- joyed, by favour of her Majesty, the use of Sheen Lodge, in Richmond Park, as his residence.

div.head: STEPNEY PETITION.
div.p: THE STEPNEY PETITION.

Judgment was given on Wednesday on the Stepney election petition. Mr. Justice Cave (delivering the deci- sion of himself and Mr. James Williams) said the "Step- ney Fathers" card was about as injudicious a thing as possible, but the Court held that the allegations against Mr. Isaacson, jun., in respect of it had failed. The charges of corrupt practices had also failed. There was undoubtedly a false return of expenses to some extent, but he thought the error might have been inadvertent, and on the whole the illegalities were so trifling that they should grant relief to the persons who asked for it, and order that Mr. Isaacson should retain his seat and have half his costs paid out of the £l,OOO deposited in court.

div.head: -THE SMALLPDX HOSPITAL.
div.p: -THE SMALLPDX HOSPITAL.

Sir,—Having heard of complaints as to the treatment received by the patients at the Smallpox Hospital in Dallam-lane, I feel it my duty to contradict these in- correct statements. Having been an inmate four weeks suffering from the disease,l am able to inform the public that the sufferers are exceedingly well treated, the greatest consideration being shown for the Datients,both by the medical officers and the nurses in attendance, everything possible being done to alleviate their suffer- ings. Personally, I desire to thank the officials for the kindness I have experienced at their hands, and add a word of praise for the manner in which the institution is conducted.—Yours truly, 106, Pierpoint-st., December 23rd, 1892.
JOHN MAHONEY.

THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE RURAL SANI- TARY AUTHORITY. Sir,-1 am informed on the most reliable authority that the smallpox epidemic in the town is taking its welcome departure. The fresh cases are few—there is ample accommodation fcr all the probable cases at the Hospital ' • so that the disease may said to be now thoroughly in hand and under control. After all the expense to the ratepayers, and the sufferings of the re- vaccinated, it is melancholy and deplorable to think that the foul complaint is allowed to go rampant and unchecked at our threshold through the inaction of the Rural Sanitary Authority. There are now three cases off the Liverpool Road just outside the borough boundary in the most insanitary, crowded, and filthy streets, where the patients cannot be isolated ; and the Rural Authority cannot remove to hospital, because it has not got one. Yet if these three cases are not quickly re- moved there may be thirty in a short time. The hun- dreds of men emplosed at Houghton's, Monks Sz Co's, the White Lead and Carbolic works, who go along Liverpool-road to their homes in the borough, may be the cause at any moment, of a fresh outbreak in our midst. It will be iniquitous and criminal if the Rural Sanitary Authority do not rouse itself to its sense of its grave responsibilities—cease its squabbling,s with the Warring- ton Sanitary Committee, and come to arrangements for the hospital isolation of its infectious diseases ; and fail- ing to do this, it is incumbent on the Warrington Cor- poration to 'appeal immediately to the Local Government Board in self-defenee.--Yours truly, December 24th, 1892. SENTINEL.

div.head: " HOUSE" UPON SAND.
div.p: A " HOUSE" UPON SAND.

" It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks."—Acts, lx. 5. Sir,—Your report of the sermon preached last Sunday, the nth inst., on the occasion of the re-opening of Bold- st.,Chapel, affords some very instructive reading to those who have the time to think, as well as read aboat it. First let me say that when a sermon is published it be- comes a fair matter for fair criticism. Then I say that had this very foolish sermon been submitted to the censorship of say Dr. Dallinger—or Frank Ballard—it would never have seen the light in its present form. When speakina on religious matters it is quite admissible —nay inevitable—that we should talk about things of which we know nothina,but believe much ; when speak- ing of matters scientific we should confine ourselves to what we know. The preacher's reference to" ancestral maggots " was not needed to show that he was not an Evolutionist. What, then, is he ? A special creationist ? Dare he, before an audience of average capacity and acquire- ments, venture to uphold the discarded dogma of special creation, now so generally dismissed by the more en- lightened leaders of his own connection ? These " maggots" are entirely of the rev, gentleman's own breeding, they exist only in his own brain. When a man leaves the vague generalities of hortation to attack the best results of the best science of the day, he is liable to make himself and his subject ridiculous. Surely, in this selfish, money-worshiping world, there are abuses to attack and wrongs to be righted, enough to occupy all the pulpits in the country. Now, whilst disclaiming the title of materialist for myself, I beg to say that the definition of this offensive appellation depends much upon the date of its applica- tion. I give the rev.gentleman credit for so much enlight- enment and general knowledge of natural phenomena as would have earned him the title of materialist three hundred years ago ! Even later than this when men hesitated to use a winnowing machine, on the plea that to raise the wind was the province of the Lord ; he might have fallen under grave suspicion of heterodoxy on this head ! Why men should be at such pains, and sacrifice so much of truth and consistency, to uphold this thrice borrowed Akkadio-Chaldean fable is a puzzle. But when the maintenance of the whole House depends upon the belief in this dogma the head of that House may see visions of its collapse, like one of cards, if the results of modern investigation should filter down into the understandings of congregations. Ignorance being the mother of devotiop—it would seem to be the motto of some of the clergy :—Better ignorance and devotion to fables than knowledge and the discarding of myths.— Yours, 31c.

JOHN PEERS. VOTERS AND VIVISECTION. man has a soul and a conscience—and I am far from wishing to deny either—both will be the bet- ter for occasional exercise upon subjects outside the restricted limits of the individual interests. To be oc- casionally lifted out of urselves, and to be enabled to view things apart from considerations as to our material interests, is beneficial. Upon this restless globe we are merely lodgers and should endeavour to pay for our entertaiment by leaving the world better than we found it, by the advocacy and practice of

righteousness. My present concern is with the rights of animals to immunity from torture. Now, what has the subject te do with that of the lowering of the Franchise ? Much. Every parliamentary voter may be called upcn to give in his decision, through the ballot-box, upon the ques- tion of vivisection. It rest upon him then as a personal reeponsibilty to know at least, the elements of the ques- tion. As I wish to bring the meaning of vivisection as vividly as possible before the mind's eye of four readers let me pray the present reader to imagine himself to be an animal caged and awaiting the ordeal of scientific torture. If the reader has sufficient imagination to put himself in the place of the victim—to see himself taken and bound in a constrained position on a table—gagged to prevent his cries—and some sensitive part of his body cut into—the devilish drug curare given him to render him quieter but more susceptible of pain—his nerves ex- cited to agony by electricity—he may then form some small conception of what is meant by vivisection. Would the reader think man had the right to treat him in such a fashion ? The law forbids the perpetration of such revolting cruelties upon man ; why then should it be allowed in the case of animals Nature dooms all living things to die once, the scientific torturer dooms his victims to the mortal agonies of a thousand deaths, which he artificially pro- longs, in order to note, with unpitying eye, the anguished quiverings of its tortured frame. But hear what an eye- witness (up to this favourable to the practice) has tosay en this question. Ile was invited to witness some stock experiments on living creatures, especially frogs. I did so. A pledge of absolute secrecy was demanded and given ; and he who so demanded was wise in his generation. One afternoon I descended into hell. Of what I saw I may not speak, save that it was eloquent enough of what had been done before, and would be done afterwards. I came out into the sunshine of the outer world sickened, shocked, and revolted beyond measure ; the twittering of free and happy birds seemed but to thrill the air with tremulous agony—and such agony so miserably meaningless and inexpressibly pitiful was that I had left behind." • • • " I am con- scious that, in the words of Mrs. Besant, some prices are too dear to pay for life ;' " and the licensed dissec- tion of living animals is one of them "—Amos Waters in the "Agnostic Journal," June 25th, 1892. I am almost afraid of saying more ; no words of mine can add force to the above, which is eloquent both in what it says and what it leaves unsaid on this painful subject. But in this matter we electors have a plain duty to perform, to endeavour to clear the land of this stain of licensed cruelty. If we allow others to commit these crimes in our name, we are, if not the actual criminals, accessories to the crime. The only right these scientific torturers have to perpetrate their horrible brutalities is the right which the electors of the United Eingdom have given them by license. But what moral right had we to give this immoral right to them ? That the vivisection of animals will ultimately lead to the • u EIL BLESSING TO MOTFIERA. div.head: TIM" GYM."
div.p: TIM" GYM."

The " certain " eight who have been selected to play in the shield competition, commencing on the 7th of next month, are :—J. Podmore, W. Walsh, E. Warren, J. Mottram, J. Holmes, G. Vernon, and F. Benion ; and A. Dickens has been selected as a reserve man. The editor of the " Gymnasium," has been suffering from a prophetic presentiment, and he calmly assures us that Warrington will get" knocked" in the first round. Had he been a weather prophet he perhaps could have added a little inform ation as to whether he knew for certain or not.

By the way a person wants to know "what do they do at the'Gym.' when the gas goes out." From what I know of it mast of the officials blow down the pipes for a short time. Anyhow, some people who know about it say that now the eight are in for hard work, an absence ofj" gas" is desirable. It won't do to allow the defect which has existed this week in the pipes to con- tinue.
The exercises for the competition are " dumbells, parallel bars, and high jumping. The marks will be taken collectively, and the maxinaum number is 20 per man.

I see that the National Physical Recreation Society have forwarded circulars on to the "Gym." offering diplomas for physical tests. To earn one of these dip- lomas a man has to hoist his chin eight times over the bar, and jump 3ft. 61n. For a bronze medal he has to raise his chin 13 times above the bar and jump 4ft. Sin. The ladies have to raise their chins once above the bar (this chin exercise should come so naturally to all ladies) and jump 3 feet. For a bronze medal tkey have to jump 31t. 2in. and raise the chin three times above the bar. The boys have to jump 31t. 6in. and pull above the bar five times for a diploma, and jump four inches more and pull over the bar eight times for a medal. The conduc- tor has been made awarder of distinctions.
IMPUDENT ROBBERY BY BOYS AT WIDNES.

• • -- - --- At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs.:J. Brock and G. Pilkington, six boys, named Andrew Fitzharris, Edward Hopkins, Isaac Melton, Thomas Stewart, Thomas Pointon, and William Melton, all residing in Simms cross, awl whose ages ranged from thirteen to seventeen years, were charged with stealing a cashbox, containing about £5, from a desk on the counter of a beerhouse, 55, Midwood- street, the property of Margaret Cogley. About ten o'clock on Wednesday night, the prosecutrix was sitting behind the counter reading a paper and heard someone come in. She said " Well," but as she received no answer she went on reading her paper. A few minutes later Mrs. Cogley had occasion to go to the cashbox, which was in the desk on the counter, and found that it had been taken away. When arrested by Police-con- , stable Messenger on Friday morning all the boys pleaded guilty.—The lad Isaac Melton and another boy named John Conroy were charged with stealing a glass bottle of biscuits from the shop of William Merriman, grocer, 12, Ann-street, en the sth inst.—Tne bench dismissed the charge against Conroy, and Superintendent Keighley informed the court that they had not recovered any of the £5. The boys had spent the money in drink, and some of them got drunk on the whisky they bought.— Hopkins and Isaac Melton were sent to gaol for ten days, . „ . . .
to be followed by four years' detention in a reformatory; Stewart was fined 10s. and Fitzharris, Pointon, and William Melton were ordered to receive nine strokes with the birchrod.

To those who mean to send Christmas cards to their friends, the Post Office has issued an order in amplifica- tion of the regulation for circulars, extending to Christ- mas cards the privilege of cheap postage. The standing rule in the Post Office Guide says : "Letters which from internal evidence appear to be intended for transmission in identical terms to several persons, and the whole or the greater part of which is produced by means of ordinary type, engraving litho- graphy, or other mechanical process, may also be sent by book post." As an instruction to local postmasters and others a notice has been supplied from the General Post Office to the effect that complimentary greetings and the name and address of the sender are to be allowed on such posted matter as season cards and the like. This has certainly not been generally unberstood, and will be welcomed by people with a limited income. An impor- tant point to remember is that the envelope must not be sealed down.
RUNCORN AND DISTRICT PERFECT THRIFT BUILDING SOCIETY.

This society was inaugurated on Fritlf-i-Y night last week by a public meeting and concert in Runcorn Public Hall. There was a good attend- Mr. P. Speakman C.C., presided and delivered a brief speech upon the advantages by thrift and economy. In the course of the evening Mt. W. Horsley, of Harrogate, the originator of the "Per- fect Thrift" system:delivered a lecture on " How to live rent free." He remarked that no doubt everyone in Runcorn would be anxious to know how to do this, and at the outset he informed the audience that every one who joined this society would be able to obtain a house of their own without any payment whatever over and above what they are now paying as rent. Rent simply meant a sunk and lost fund : the more they paid in rent the more they lost. The man who paid £6OO in rent had not anything to show for it; but by joining this society they would get rid of that one thing rent. The society was firstly a purely co-operative workingman's building society; secondly, it could be used as a savings bank ; and lastly it gave provision for death by a free ballot at death. As a Building Society it consisted of 399 members, who are called ballot members, and who pay their subscriptions of 6d. is., and Is. ed., and 28. per week. Each sixpence represents one share, which was of the value of £lOO. In virtue of their paying subscrip- tions to the society each member was entitled to receive an appropriation by ballot of £lOO, £2OO, £3OO, or £4OO, to have a right to use this money by purchasing a house, 11,-.mses, or land and to repay the same at the rate of £6 per hundred- per year for 16 years and eight months without any interest. Property could easily be purchased in Runcorn, to yield 8 per cent., or, in other words, if a man is living in a house and paying £l2 a year as rent he can purchase the house for £2OO. Therefore, having received an appropriation of £2OO lie used that to buy the house, and then simply takes his rent of £l2 per year, either weekly, monthly, or quarterly, to the Perfect Thrift Society, and in sixteen years and eight months he had purchased his house by the payment of rent alone. This would go on until every member has had a ballot and made his repay- ments as before stated. Again, if a member did not wish to use his appropriation, he had the right to sell it to anyone or to the society, and the society's price was £8 with all subscriptions returned. TMs was better than five per cent investment. If a member does not wish to wait for his ballot he can purchase one, two, three, or four hundred pounds from the society at a deferred payment of say £75 for £2OO, which would mean an annual payment of £l6 10s. He would be able to purchase a house tor £2OO, that would produce £l2 per year rent, which would only necessitate his adding £4 ios. a year to enable Mtn to become his own landlord as a purchase member. Probably he would be able to purchase a house for £2OO which would yield £l6 a year If so it would only cost him 10s. per year as a purchase member to become possessed of a £2OO house. In addi- tion to these advantages the society gave a free ballot at death, which meant that should a member die his representatives would become entitled to £lOO, £2OO, £3OO, or £4OO, in the same way as if his number had been drawn at an ordinary ballot meeting. The society : was a purely local society managed entirely by the i members themselves. All officers must be members.
THE PROPOSED PURCHASE OF THE RUNCOItN WATERWORKS.

A special meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners was held on Monday afternoon, at the Town Hall, to affix the seal of the Board to a petition re the Runcorn Water Bill. There were present Messr3. Wiswall (chairman), J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, D. Bisbrown, S. Taylor, W. Hankinson, H. Coward, T. Lea, and J. W. Lighthurn ; Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), and Mr. E. Marshall (secretary). Mr. Lake explained that the draft clauses of the Bill had been gone through by the Parliamentary Committee, and sundry alterations made. The last day for the presenta- tion of the petition to the House of Commons for leave to , bring in the Bill was Wednesday, and it was their duty ' to get it in as soon as possiwe, so that, the .nearing or the Bill might be on an early date. It was a case of urgency. After some discussion it was unanimously decided', on the motion of Mr. Pritchard, seconded by Mr. Fisher, that the Board's seal be affixed to the peti- tion. Mr. Taylor took no part in the proceedings. Mr. Bisbro4n desired to know when it was likely that the meeting of ratepayers would be held to consider the question. Mr. Lake replied that as soon as they received the reports of the gentlemen appointed to in- spect the works of the company and the books, the ' meeting would be called. The sooner this was done the better for all parties.

FOOTBALL.

Before proceeding to the usual bulletin of sporting facts, I will take the opportunity of wishing all our readers a bright and joyous Christmas ; and I couple with it the hope that Warrington F.C. will receive a few more anonymous contributions as Christmas presents! Au! The P.D., with his smiling, open countenance, also demurely tenders me the following note for insertion : " Sur, i tak upon mi self the dooty of squirming u a round robbin From the Comps, arsking u, on hour be half, 2 request those Far foot ball hers 2 postpone their matcLes next week; failing which we hope they Will Not break more legs and eds than necessary. We don't want no copy next week—don't we men of letters ?"

Warrington first team had a tough game with Barrow, at Barrow on Saturday. The team was an excellent ono, the only conspicious player absent being Jolley. The turf was exceedinzly heavy and did a great deal towards preventing the" runners" of bah teams fulfilling their duties.

The one feature which characterized the whole of the matches on Saturday was that darkness spread its sombre cloak over both football and players long before the matches were really at an end, and many of the spectators were inclined to hum the lines respecting the shadows of the evening drawing across the sky.

Within about a quarterof an hour after play had been commenced the players were scarcely recognizable. With the exception of some really clever passing between Bate, Evans, and Lawless, In the first portion of the match, the game was conspicuous for nothing except some hard forward play. The match all round was a fairly equally contested one,the most conspicuous players on the Warrington side being that of Nevins and Berry.

A "gate" of the average strength assembled on the ground in Wilderspool to see the game between War- rington ." A" team and Failsworth Old Boys. If the match wasn't altogether interesting it certainly lacked nothing in the way ot an amusing exhibition. uhough both teams played a game full of laughable discrepan- cies, Warrington certainly met with more than their match in everything except the forwards. Davies and Jolley took great care to preserve the reputation of that portion of the team.

F. Flampson who, I think, is an introduction didn't by any means distinguish himself at three-quarters. Often he proved that he could play an excellent garn:,‘ but either from nervousness, or indisposition, he mulled several times, and allowed the visitors to get the ball dangerously near the line. He may be a good three- quarter, but it was perhaps hardly advisable to place him in such a responsible position, at least until he gets used to playing before an "audience."

During the whole of the match the visitors proved themselves too much for the home men—not because they were really a stronger team, but beeause those in responsible positions in the Warrington team didn't come up to the " mark." The ball was in tne Warrington domain almost the whole time, and if it hadn't been for the quick, experienced, and determined play of Tony, Davies, and Jolley, why, I'm afraid the good old team would have been considerably "lammed." They showed no sign of scoring until near the end of the game, and the spectators commenced to howl in dispair " now Warrington, liven up."

The "old boys" had scared a goal and a minor before half-time, and afterwards they made several really good attempts to augment. When Warrington scored it had grown quite dark,and how they obtained the try or how they augmented it to a goal, I could not see. For the last five minutes of play all that was descernible was a little dark object spinning about the field with larger shadowy objects chasing it. This state of things made me chuckle,for it reminded me of an extraordinary thing I saw happen at Widnes some years ago.

The time is drawing nigh when the junior clubs will decide who shall have Mr. P. Davies's silver cup. The Rangers and the Parish Church Club met on Saturday for the purpose of helping on a solution; and, much to the surprise of everyone. the Churchmen caused the result to form an argument in favour of their possession of the cup. They won by two tries to one.

The association team met with a small adventure on Saturday. They journeyed to Liverpool for the purpose of meeting the Caledonians. But just as they were proceeding through Liverpool some m )re footballers came along and asked them "Whither away ?"and verily, when they said, " to the Caledonians," the strangers faces said " Yea, we do wither away." Then their tongue said" Why, blemrae, the Caledonians are bank- rupt."

This turned out to be only too true ; their financiers had, so to speak, shot the accounts anywhere but at goal. The strangers, who were the 3rd Volunteer Bat- talion Club, said the club they ought to have met had also " gone to smash," and they therefore proposed the Warrington team should play wick them instead, and the Warrington Association men agreed ; and then they went and licked them.

On Thursday night the Liverpool Association took in- to consideration the protests which had been forwarded by the Warrington Association Club, as a result of their match played at Liverpool with the Liverpool Printers on Dec. 10th. The Association,after hearin.he protests decided in favour of Warrington, and ordered the match to be replayed on January 7th.

Last Saturday, the Warrington Reserve in their usual playful fashion chalked up a score of six to one against Lymm Reserve. This afternoon they will play Widnes Parish Church at Warrington,when a good game is anti- cipated.

It was a big match, and the Widnes team was being terribly beaten. The game was approaching its end, but it had grown quite dark. Just when play was near the visitors' posts, a little dark object was seen to dart through the thick of the players and go ahead. The visitors didn't see anyone kick the ball, but they fol- lowed it up, as they thought. On, on it went, the whole team helter skelter after it. Near the other end of the Beld the best runner of the pack caught up to it and grabbed at it. But he dropped it instantly, and the ob- ject still continued its course ; it was a Skye terrior. In the meantime the home men had got the ball over the line, and the try was allowed. About the most 'interesting Match in connection with the Lancashire Cur) Competition occurred on Saturday, when St. Helens Recs. met Swinton and were beaten by three tries to nothing. The game was exceedingly ex- citing, and the result was unexpected to those who have watched this seasons performances of the Recs.

div.head: SAVAGE ASSAULTS ON WIDNES
div.p: SAVAGE ASSAULTS ON WIDNES
PUBLICANS.

On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. J. Brock and G. Pilkington, two brothers named James John Tobin and John Tobin, both re- siding in Sankey-st., was brought up in custody charged with unlawfully wounding Owen Lenchen, manager of the Waterloo Vaults, on Saturday last. About half-past ten o'clock on Saturday night the pri- soners were at the bar of the house and began quarrel- ling with another man. The prosecutor put James out of the house. When in the street James kicked Lenchen very severely, and his brother threw a brick at prosecu- tor, which struck him on the forehead and inflicted a severe wound.—Dr. Hutchinson who is attending the injured man, deposed that Lenchen was suffering from a confused wound on the forehead, one and three-quar- ter inches long in one direction and one and a half in another. He had also been badly kicked, and at pre- sent was confined to his bed. He was not free from danger to his life.—On the application of Superintendent Keighley, the prisoners were remanded until Monday next.—At the same court, a man named Richard Brad- ley, of no fixed abode, was brought up on remand charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Samuel Hirst, landlord of the Commercial Hotel, Appleton, an Saturday, the 19th ult., by kicking him and breaking his arm. The prosecutor stated that on the night in question the prisoner was creating a disturbance in the house, and threatened to knock witness's eye out with a glass. Bradley refused to leave and prosecutor put him out, whereupon the prisoner and a companion attacked him in brutal fashion, hitting him with their fists and hicking him, breaking his right arm. Bradley was committed for trial at the sessions.

It is reported from Berlin of the first hackney carriage provided with an electric light, that the novelty has bad such an effect on the cab drivers in general that they are all demanding the new light for their carriages.

PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLL—SeIIIIO/19 in be- half of these schools were preached in the Parish Church on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. S. F. Bennetts, curate, and in the evening by the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A. The offertories amounted to £7 7s. 9d. SOCIAL GATHBRING.—On Monday evening, the second entertainment in connection with Mr. Tear's night school was given in the National School, when there was a very large and appreciative audience. The Rev. S. C. Barm- by. 8.A., presided. The programme consisted of vocal and instrumental music, recitations, -

THE NATIONAL GIRLS''SCHOOL.—d7I Monday a concert was given by the girls attending this school, the chair man being Mr. H. B. Blogg, vicar. The entertainmetn comprised songs, recitations, a •short cantata, &c., which.were all well rendered and much enjoyed. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS—Socialism was the subject of a lecture delivered by the Rev. C. Craddock sr the meeting on Wednesday, to a fair number of mem- bers and others. HELSBY.

PRIZIa DISTRIBUTION.—The annual concert given by the children attending the church day schools was held on Thursday evening, and there was a large attendance. A capital programme of songs and character sketches was very creditably gone through by the young people, to the evident enjoyment of those present. During the evening the Vicar, who presided, presented the prizes to those who had been regular in their attendance. Twenty-nine children out of an average of 82 children, had made 400 attendances out of a possible 419 for the year just closed, while two boys, Arthur Jeff and Alfred Ellams, had not missed school once during tho twelve months. A prize was also given to the " best boy, and best girl," on the vote of the children.

div.head: RECORDER OF LIVERPOOL AND MEDICAL DESPOTISM."
div.p: THE RECORDER OF LIVERPOOL AND MEDICAL DESPOTISM."

VACCINATION A" FILTHY AND POISONOUS RITE." Mr. Charles Ef. Hopwood, M.P.,Recorder of Liverpool, has sent to Mr. A. W. Hutton, who recently delivered a lecture at Chiswick on "Compulsory Vaccination," at which the hon. gentleman presided, aremarkably strong and vigorous letter on the subject. Writing from Liver- pool, he says :—" I hope the lecture will convert many. I am quite sure it will strengthen on one side those who doubt, and confirm the resolution of those who have taken the determination to oppose compulsory vaccina- tion. I look forward to the emancipation of my countrymen from this medical depotism at an early date. This healthy struggle for liberty has come fr)m below; and the thoughtlessness of the (so-called' scientific world, who have given in their cohesion te quackery. will be reproved by the untaught manliness and courage of parents who, prompted by love of their off- 1 spring, have dared to think and to suffer in defence of , their children. Our victory will be in favour of true science, for nothing opposes so blind, so 'ethargic an obstacle to research and advance as a law which enacts and stereotypes a false or doubtful remedy. It has been a hard battle to face the authority of law arid the slavish ' subjection of middle-class fears to the authority of medical men. These at one time have preached that inoculation was the remedy, and at another they joined in making inoculation punishable. They promise no absolute protection by cowpox once inserted. They now say that we must practice the filthy and poisonous rite oftener and in greater quantity. They have as little foundation for the one error as they had for the other. some, ho wever, of the noblest of them are now on our side. Let our cry be for liberty for ourselves and others. and to free science from the shams which encompass it."

div.head: BURNLEY VACANCY.
div.p: THE BURNLEY VACANCY.

The Hon. Philip Stanhope addressed a meeting of the General Council of the Burnley Liberal Association on Thursday evening with a view to his adoption as the Liberal candidate for the borough at the ensuing elec- tion. Mr. Stanhope spoke on the subject of Home Rule and on the general programme of Liberal Reform. At the close of his speech a resolution was enthusiastically , passed adopting him as the candidate of the party. :4K 1.§1C4

div.head: STATION MASTER.
div.p: STATION MASTER.

After holding the position of stationmaster at Bank Quay since 1875, the duties of which he has discharged with much satisfaction, not only to the London and North-western Railway Company, but to passengers generally, Mr. Ashurst the station- master at Bank Quay, retires at the end of this month into private life. He will carry with him the best wishes of a large circle of friends he has made in the, town and district. Mr. Ashurst is a very old servant of the company, having been a stationmaster for 35 years. I He was appointed the first stationmaster at Rainford, when that line was opened between Garston and South- port in January 1858. In June 1867, he was transferred to St. Helens, to more important duties as stationmaster and clerk in charge. In June 1875, he was selected tg take up the still more important charge of the stations at Warrington, namely, Bank Quay (high and low level) and Arpley, where he has remained up to the present time. Fortunately, no accident of a serious nature has occurred during that time in the district over which his supervision extends. Mr. Ashurst has done much to raise the moral tone of railway men in Warrington, having opened and carried on a mission especially for their good in a room over Arpley Railway Station, and latterly, owing to the liberality of the ladies and gentle- men of Warrington and its suburbs,a female missionary has been engaged to visit them in their homes, to ren- der help in case of sickness, as well as, where necessary, to induce them to attend a place of worship. For 14 Years he has been one of the teachers of the St. Paul's Sunday school, as well as one of the sidestuen of the church, and he is also a prominent Freemason, now occupying the chair or the Gilbert Greenall Lodge as W.M. A more industrious, painstaking, and conscien- tious man it would be difficult to find, and the Railway Company and public will fully realize the loss of a most useful man to the service in which he was employed.
L.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

TABLEAUX VIVANTS AT THE THEATRE. As the public will be already aware,circumstances have been most unpropitious for the fortunes of the Warrington Musical Society. During their mirrent season, they having been compelled in consequence of the epidemic, to abandon two concerts, as well as their rehearsals. Thursday night was the date fixed for one of the concerts, and the Royal Court Theatre had been engaged for the occasion. This being the case,and there having been such a decided decline in the epidemic, a number of ladies and gentlemen connected with the Musical Society, and others, conceived that in order to pay the rent of the theatre for the evening, and do something for the funds of the society, in what has proved to them, an unrernunerative year, it might not be a bad thing to give an exhibition of tablsaux vivants. The idea was carried out, and on Thursday evening the exhibition was given, with vocal music by various ar- ti,tes,Mrs.J. P. Reynolds accompanying on the piano. The audience was not a large one,indeetl, much smaller than was commensurate with the rAerit of the entertainment. The first item on the programme was a gart song, "The miller's wooing," which was very pleasingly sung, this , being followed by a song by Mrs. Dobson, "Come, lasses I and lads." and tableaux, these constituting a most picturesque series of views, illustrative of a rural May festival, and being loudly applauded by the captivated audience. Mr. W. H. Wallington next sang, " Philip the falconer" in excellent style ; and the quaint song was fitly followed by a quaint tableaux, illustrative of a passage from high life in a past age—with which engrav- ings from a famous picture have made the public well acquainted—entitled "The minuet," showing a juvenile musician, quite of the Little Lord Fauntleroy type of boyish beauty, seated on a table, and playing the violin, while his elder and juvenile sisters are practising steps in grave, demure style in accompaniment. Mr. R. T. Fairclough gave the next song, "A cup of tea," in an effective manner, the tableaux presented in connec- tion with this being " A Japanese tea party," , and representing a number of Japanese ladies seated on the floor in free and easy style, enjoying a cup of the fragrant decoction, after the fashion of their country. The song was accompanied with a vocal chorus and the clinking of tea-cups, which made it much more realistic. Miss B. Fanshawe, sang in good style, and with quite dramatic effect, " Angus Macdonald." Her song was followed by tableaux repre- senting " The sleeping beauty." " Where are you going to my pretty maid ?" was decidedly the best executed part song of the evening, and the tableaux illustrating this were of a really exquisite character, exciting much applause. "In the cloisters " which Mr. R. Eccles sang in very nice style, was succeeded by the tableaux "Catching and caught." Then came the interval, and the second part commenced with tableaux, Noblesse oblige," or " Two more couples wanted." , Thereafter appeared Mr. W. H. Wallington who sang in fine style "To Anthea," and was encored, repeating the song. Then were introduced tableaux "Recreation in a Cloister," and " aris Eminence for audience," in which ancient monks were depicted as going through musical ' exercises in one of their cloistral chambers. A trio " Q.teen of the night," by Mrs. Dobson, Miss Fanshawe, ' and Mr. Eccles, was beautifully sung and much applauded. Then amusing tableaux " Forbidden fruit " illustrated a courting scene between a policeman and a kitchenmaid and the sudden discovery of their proceedings by her mistress. A prettily rendered song by Miss Jeans, with a subdued chorus, and accompany- ing tableaux, "Love in the Moon constituted the next presentment. A song and tableaux,"No thank you,Tom," followed.the former being excellently sung with a quaint expression peculiarly suited to the sentiment, and being encored, with the result of the repetition of the last. verse. A part song and tableaux " Gipsy Life "concluded-the entertainment, which we may say was artistically a steiking success, the manner in which the various personage in the tableaux preserved their statuesqueimmobility, shuwing that there is a poetry of motionlessness as well as a poetry of motion. Mr. F. H. Crossley had the grouping and posing of the figures, and had ample occasion to congratulate himself on his suc- cess. The ladies connected with the entertainment had been assiduously sewing for some time, preparing the costumes, with, we may say, the happiest result. There was one drawback to the success of the entertainment, and that was as to the curtaining of the stage. The curtains could not always be drawn close, and the part- ing between them disclosed much of what was going on behind in the preparation for the tableaux. On one occasion two of the performers were subjected to a try- ing ordeal, in consequence of one the curtains sticking fast when it was about to be drawn across to close the scene, and the artistes having to sit motionless and pre- serve one expression of countenance for some time , longer than they intended. The curtains, moreover, : were too thin; and did not perfectly conceal what was taking place behind, even when they could be closely drawn. The following, took part in the tableaux : Messrs. W. E. Atkin, Leonard Smith, C. R. Crossley, W. Dutton, Bolder°, E. L. Fletcher, James Fairclouah, B. Fairclough, and D. Fairclougli, Master L. Fairclough, Miss Smith, the Misses Nunnerley, Misses Mabel, Molly, J., and N. Fairelough, and Miss Fairhurst. Several of the gentlemen's costumes were kindly supplied by Mrs. Long, of Thelwall Heyes, The lime light apparatus was efficiently manipulated by Messrs...E. W. Reynolds, and H. N. Houghton.
LATEST NE WS.
THE NORTHAMPTION MURDER.

The trial of Andrew Macrae, for the alleged murder of Annie Pritchard, was continued at Northampton yester- day. A further letter from the murdered woman to her sisters and brothers was read. Dr. Milligan declared that some bones submitted to him by the police com- prised two end bones of human fingers, and portions of other bones had saw marks upon them. Amongst the ashes submitted to him were bone ashes. The condition in which the body was found was consistent with death on July 20th.--similar evidence was given by Dr. Bond, of London, who said, however, that the, bone seemed to have been sawn by a finer saw than that found at the warehouse.

THE NORTH MEATH PETTITON.
DAVITT UNSEATED.

At the sitting of the Court, yesterday, Jr. Justice Andrews and Mr. Justice Johnson gave judgaent in Mr. Pierce Maliony's petition against the retina of Mr. Michael Davitt for Forth Meath. Their lordslips decided that Mr. Davitt's election was void on the ground of undue exercise of spiritual influence by the ishop and clergy of the diocese. Mr. Davitt is, therefore unseated.
THE LIBERATOR BUILDING SWIETY.

--- THE CHARGES OF FRAUD AND FORCERY. At Bow-st., yesterday, James William abbs, ex- Mayor of Croydon, and Henry Granville Wrigh,solicitor surrendered to their bail to meet the various clarges of forgery, larceny, and fraudulent conversion i connec- tion with the affairs of the Liberator Building Society, now in liquidation, with many of the bodies it inaneed. Further evidence was given by people who swre that the signatures to the bills of exchange purportitg.to be drawn by them were forgeries. The case was adourned.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—Thera Is A firm tone in the market, but decidedly less Eastern trade is being done, and for other markets no improv, met is noticeable. Cotton is quieter. Futures have not improved upon opening rates, and American spot is the turn easier, though Dhollerah has been advanced 1-16 d. Business has not exceeded 8,00 bales. Yarns are strong and dearer on the week, though cot- ton has not altered materially in spot prices. There are, how- ever. fewer resales offering, and their disappearance tends to greater strength. The den md, however, is no very vigor- ous, but sellers have a tight grip. In cloth there is less demand and despite the reduced output a groat deal ot stock can yet be founsi in various quarters. II dian inquiry of a workable character has tailed off considerably. No increase is noticeable for China, and the vo:ume of business for the smaller foreign outlets Is not perceptibly greater. The home houses place few new orders, but are recexing old contracts readily.

COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of The Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER, will be holden at the CASTLE OF CEIESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 2nd day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pris- oners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 2no 1r of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will b. 5 Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on the 4th day of Janu- ary next, at Eleven o'clock in the tOrt.n. The hear- ing of all Appeals arising within the Hunorcdß of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Nortliwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners corn- witted from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attend- ance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD PO'ETS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 12th December, 1892.

THE BLACKBURN MURDER. DATE OF EXECUTION. The high sheriff of the county has fixed Tuesday. January 3rd, as the date for the execution of Cross Duckworth, who, on December 13th, at the Liverpool Assizes, was found guilty of the murder of Aliee flumes, at Witton-park, Blackburn, but recommended to mercy. The execution will take place at Walton Gaol, Billington being the executioner. A GANG OF SWINDLERS BROKEN UP SYSTEMATIC PILFERING. An accomplished gang of swindlers was broken up at the Old Bailey on Wednesday. Thirteen men who had carried on a system of fraud in various parts of the country, taking shops and obtaining gcods on credit by means of mutual references, were shown to have robbed provision merchants and others to the extent of some thousands of pounds, and the Common Sergeant passed exemplary sentences upon them. Eleven of the r..g,ues go into penal servitude for terms ranging from three to- ten years, and the remaining two have to undergo. imprisonment for twelve and nine months. • _
